techniques.name: Copper working & smelting

arrivals.note: comparably early; priority between Balkans, Anatolia and Iran is debated
native copper hammered and annealed, never smelted or cast; some dates reach c. 6500 BCE
small knives and awls; large-scale Chinese metallurgy only from c. 1900 BCE
arrives with Beaker package
hammered gold foil precedes copper; copper smelting established during the 1st millennium BCE
earlier Agadez dates (c. 2000 BCE) are disputed
c. 600-800 CE; technology carried by sea from Ecuador/Peru

techniques.rule: Smelted/cast copper or bronze in Mesoamerica ⇒ after c. 700 CE (mostly 900-1521). North American native-copper sheet work (Old Copper, Hopewell, Mississippian) is hammered, not cast. Any cast copper-alloy object in Britain ⇒ after c. 2400 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: Cast copper has mould seams, sockets, and thick sculptural forms; hammered native copper is thin sheet, rolled beads, riveted or folded, with a lumpy laminated look. Pure copper weathers to red-brown and green; bronze to smoother olive/dark green.
techniques.blurb: Copper was the first metal worked at scale, but the three big American metalworking zones followed very different paths: the Great Lakes stayed with cold-hammering for millennia, the Andes developed smelting and alloys independently, and Mesoamerica received metallurgy late and ready-made from the south.

techniques.name: Tin bronze

arrivals.note: Cornish tin makes Britain an early full-tin-bronze region
arsenical copper dominates the Old Kingdom; tin bronze normal from the Middle Kingdom

arrivals.place: Mainland Southeast Asia (Ban Chiang, Ban Non Wat)
arrivals.note: date debated between c. 2000 and c. 1000 BCE; short chronology now favoured
bronze and iron arrive together from Korea
independent tin-bronze tradition; spread empire-wide by the Inca after c. 1450
leaded tin bronze, lost-wax cast

techniques.rule: Tin-bronze object ⇒ not before c. 3000 BCE anywhere; in China not before c. 1900 BCE; in Japan not before c. 300 BCE; in the Andes not before c. 600 CE; in sub-Saharan West Africa not before c. 800 CE. Japan and most of Africa have no separate 'Bronze Age' before iron.
techniques.lookFor: Golden-brown where clean, smooth dark-green or black patina where buried. Arsenical copper looks similar in a photo, so use form: socketed axes, long swords and thin-walled vessels need true bronze.
techniques.blurb: Alloying copper with about 10% tin gave a harder, more castable metal and created long-distance tin trade. The date it becomes normal differs by more than three thousand years between regions, which makes 'is this bronze?' a strong where-and-when clue.

techniques.name: Chinese piece-mould ritual bronzes

arrivals.note: regional styles south of the Central Plains
taotie-covered vessels with first inscriptions
long cast inscriptions; birds replace taotie

end.note: ritual vessel sets fade under the Han; later 'archaic' bronzes are Song-Qing antiquarian revivals

techniques.rule: Bronze ding/gui/jue/zun with taotie masks or leiwen spirals ⇒ China c. 1600-200 BCE (eras 1750 BCE to 250 BCE). Long inscriptions inside the vessel ⇒ Western Zhou or later (after c. 1050 BCE). Inlaid gold/silver or turquoise on bronze ⇒ Eastern Zhou/Han (c. 600 BCE-200 CE).
techniques.lookFor: Thick-walled vessels on three or four legs, crisp relief in registers, vertical flanges where mould sections met, symmetrical animal mask (two eyes, horns, no lower jaw). No hammered sheet, no soldered-on parts.
techniques.blurb: Unlike the West, Bronze Age China cast vessels in ceramic section moulds rather than by lost wax, which is why decoration is laid out in panels divided by flanges. Lost wax appears in China only around the 6th century BCE.

techniques.name: Lost-wax casting

arrivals.note: small solid figures early; large hollow casts common in the Late Period
bangles cast by lost wax; the site's start date (c. 1200-700 BCE) is debated
hollow-cast life-size bronzes begin in the 6th c. BCE
supplements piece-moulds from the Spring and Autumn period
origin of the West African tradition is debated
arrives from lower Central America

techniques.rule: Lost-wax cast gold/copper in Mesoamerica ⇒ after c. 900 CE (mostly Postclassic 1200-1521). West African cast brass heads/plaques ⇒ after c. 850 CE and mostly 1200-1900. Life-size hollow bronze statue in the Mediterranean ⇒ after c. 550 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: One-off sculptural forms with undercuts, fine wax-thread detail (false filigree, coiled wire look), no mould seams. Hollow casts show core pins or patches.
techniques.blurb: A wax model is invested in clay, melted out and replaced by metal. The idea is very old in the Near East and South Asia, reached China surprisingly late, and was developed separately in the northern Andes, from where it travelled north to Mexico.

techniques.name: West African lost-wax brass & bronze (Igbo-Ukwu, Ife, Benin)

arrivals.note: naturalistic heads, 12th-15th c.
court casting guild; tradition credits a caster from Ife
small cast brass weights, c. 1400-1900
rectangular relief plaques c. 1500s-1600s, fed by Portuguese brass manillas

techniques.rule: Naturalistic Ife head ⇒ c. 1200-1450 (era 1000-1250 or 1250-1500). Benin plaque ⇒ 1500-1750 era; any Benin piece showing Portuguese (long hair, helmets, guns, crossbows) ⇒ after 1485. Thick heavy Benin heads with high beaded collars and wing-like projections ⇒ 18th-19th c.
techniques.lookFor: Ife: life-size idealised faces with fine vertical striations, zinc-brass or nearly pure copper. Benin: high-relief plaques with stippled quatrefoil background, coral-bead regalia, leopards, mudfish. Igbo-Ukwu: intricate surfaces of tiny loops, insects and ropework.
techniques.blurb: Igbo-Ukwu's 9th-century leaded bronzes are astonishingly intricate and locally sourced; Ife and Benin later cast in brass, with Benin's output booming once European brass arrived by sea. The British expedition of 1897 scattered the Benin corpus across world museums.

techniques.name: Iron smelting

arrivals.note: dates from c. 1800-1000 BCE claimed; possibly independent
bloomery iron first; cast iron by c. 500 BCE, 1,800 years before Europe
independent invention is debated; some claim much earlier dates
no pre-Columbian smelted iron

techniques.rule: Iron or steel tool/weapon ⇒ after c. 1200 BCE in West Asia, c. 800 BCE in temperate Europe, c. 600 BCE in China, c. 550 BCE in West Africa, c. 300 BCE in Japan, c. 200 CE in southern Africa, 1492 in the Americas. Sub-Saharan Africa goes from stone straight to iron in most regions.
techniques.lookFor: Iron corrodes to orange-brown flaky rust and swollen, cracked shapes; ancient iron objects usually look lumpy and laminated. Forged (hammered) forms dominate outside China; ornate cast-iron vessels, statues and stoves are Chinese until Europe's late-medieval blast furnaces.
techniques.blurb: Smelted iron trinkets exist from the early 2nd millennium BCE in Anatolia, but iron only replaced bronze for tools and weapons after about 1200 BCE. Whether India and sub-Saharan Africa invented smelting independently is still argued.

techniques.name: Gold granulation & filigree

arrivals.note: finest dust granulation, 7th-6th c. BCE
via the steppe and Central Asia

techniques.rule: Granulated goldwork ⇒ after c. 2500 BCE; in Italy essentially after c. 700 BCE; in China after c. 300 BCE; in Korea after c. 300 CE. Microscopic 'dust' granulation in silhouettes ⇒ Etruscan 700-500 BCE (or a 19th-c. Castellani revival piece).
techniques.lookFor: Tiny gold spheres fused to a gold sheet in lines, triangles or massed fields; filigree is twisted or beaded wire soldered in scrolls. Look for a frosted, sparkling texture on earrings, pendants and fibulae.
techniques.blurb: Granulation needs invisible solder joins, a trick lost and rediscovered several times. It runs from Sumer through Egypt and the Aegean to its peak in Etruria, and east along the steppe to Han China and Silla Korea.

techniques.name: Niello

arrivals.note: whether the black inlay is true niello is debated
common on silver plate and military fittings, 1st-4th c.
Trewhiddle style, 9th c.
Renaissance pax plaques; links to the birth of engraving
snuffboxes and tableware, 18th-19th c.

techniques.rule: Black-filled engraved silver ⇒ Roman or later in Europe (after c. 1 CE); a Mycenaean-style inlaid bronze dagger ⇒ c. 1600-1400 BCE. Niello is a weak dater on its own; use it with the object type (Roman spoon, Anglo-Saxon strap-end, Renaissance pax, Russian snuffbox).
techniques.lookFor: Matte blue-black lines or fields set flush into engraved silver (sometimes gold), contrasting with the bright metal; unlike enamel it is opaque, metallic-black and never coloured.
techniques.blurb: Niello is a black sulphide of silver, copper and lead fused into engraved grooves. It appears sporadically in the Bronze Age, becomes common under Rome, and stays in use from Anglo-Saxon England to 19th-century Russia and Thailand.

techniques.name: Cloisonne enamel

arrivals.note: gold cloisonne peaks 9th-12th c.
bronze-bodied 'Jingtai blue'; first reign-marked pieces are Xuande, 1426-35
Nagoya revival; golden age c. 1880-1910

techniques.rule: Chinese cloisonne on a copper-alloy body ⇒ not before c. 1350 (era 1250-1500 at the very earliest; most is 1500-2000). Japanese cloisonne vases ⇒ almost always 1850-1920. Gold cloisonne with saints and Greek inscriptions ⇒ Byzantine c. 850-1200.
techniques.lookFor: Coloured glass paste in cells made by thin wires soldered to the surface; you can see the wire outlines around every colour patch. Chinese pieces: turquoise ground, lotus scrolls, gilt rims. Japanese: finer or hidden wires, pictorial designs, mirror-smooth.
techniques.blurb: True enamel fused in wire cells starts with a few Late Bronze Age Cypriot rings, becomes a Byzantine court art, and reaches China only under the Mongols, where it was first seen as foreign and gaudy. Do not confuse it with garnet cloisonne, which is cut stone, not glass.

techniques.name: Champleve enamel (Celtic, Mosan, Limoges)

arrivals.note: enamelled brooches and horse gear
mass production of caskets, crosses, croziers to c. 1370
grisaille and polychrome painted enamel on copper, 1470-1650
technique learned from European imports

end.note: medieval Limoges champleve workshops collapse after the 1370 sack; painted enamel takes over a century later

techniques.rule: Gilt-copper casket, cross or pyx with blue champleve enamel and applied heads ⇒ Limoges/Mosan c. 1150-1350 (era 1000-1250 or 1250-1500). Red enamel on curvilinear bronze ⇒ Iron Age Celtic/Romano-British (c. 300 BCE-200 CE). Painted enamel plaques in grisaille ⇒ after 1470.
techniques.lookFor: Enamel sits in troughs gouged out of thick copper, so the metal lines between colours are irregular in width (not uniform wires). Limoges: deep lapis blue, turquoise, white rosettes, gilded reserved figures.
techniques.blurb: Champleve is the cheap, robust cousin of cloisonne: cut recesses in bronze or copper and fill them. Celtic smiths used opaque red glass; 12th-century Mosan and Limoges workshops turned it into Europe's standard church metalwork.

techniques.name: Struck coinage

arrivals.note: separate cast-bronze tradition; round cash with square hole standard from 221 BCE
date and degree of independence debated
silver denarius from 211 BCE
imitations of Macedonian staters
Abd al-Malik's reform: text only, no images

techniques.rule: Any coin ⇒ after c. 650 BCE. Coin with a ruler's portrait ⇒ after c. 300 BCE (Hellenistic habit). Round coin with square hole ⇒ China after c. 350 BCE (or Korea/Japan/Vietnam after c. 700-1000 CE). All-script Arabic coin ⇒ after 696 CE. Milled edge / perfectly round machine-struck coin ⇒ after c. 1550-1650.
techniques.lookFor: Hand-struck coins are slightly irregular, off-centre, with high relief; Chinese cash is cast, flat, with a square hole and four characters. Greek = city emblems and gods; Roman imperial = emperor profile with Latin legend; Islamic = concentric Kufic text.
techniques.blurb: Coinage was invented at least twice: stamped electrum lumps in Lydia and cast bronze tool-shaped money in China. Alexander's successors made the royal portrait standard, and the Umayyad reform of 696 made Islamic coins purely calligraphic.

techniques.name: Silver-inlaid brass (Islamic inlaid metalwork / damascening)

arrivals.note: 'al-Mawsili' craftsmen sign ewers and basins
large blazon and inscription bands to c. 1400
made in or for Italy c. 1450-1550
blackened zinc alloy inlaid with silver
19th-c. damascene revival

techniques.rule: Brass ewer, basin, candlestick or pen box densely inlaid with silver/copper figures and Arabic bands ⇒ Islamic lands c. 1150-1500 (eras 1000-1250 and 1250-1500). Bold thuluth inscriptions with heraldic blazons ⇒ Mamluk 1250-1400. Black-and-silver bidri ⇒ India after c. 1500.
techniques.lookFor: Yellow brass surface with thin silver (and red copper) sheet hammered into recessed designs: roundels of hunters, musicians, zodiac signs, interlace, and inscription friezes. Silver is often partly lost, leaving shadowed recesses.
techniques.blurb: The Bobrinski Bucket, made in Herat in 1163, opens two and a half centuries in which inlaid brass was the luxury metalwork of the Islamic world; after the Mongol invasions the craft shifted west to Mosul, Damascus and Cairo.

techniques.name: Andean & Isthmian goldwork, tumbaga and depletion gilding

arrivals.note: lost-wax and gold-copper alloys
depletion and electrochemical gilding, gold-silver-copper alloys
replaces jade as the prestige material c. 300-700 CE
fine lost-wax gold mostly 1200-1521

end.note: indigenous court goldwork ends with the Spanish conquests; most was melted down

techniques.rule: Gold or gilt-copper object from Mesoamerica ⇒ after c. 800-900 CE (Maya Classic art has jade, not gold). Costa Rican/Panamanian gold ⇒ after c. 300 CE. Andean sheet gold ⇒ any time after c. 1500 BCE, so use style (Chavin fanged faces, Moche, Sican masks c. 900-1100, Inca figurines).
techniques.lookFor: Tumbaga looks pinkish or patchy where copper shows through a thin golden skin. Andean work favours hammered sheet, repousse and mechanical joins; Colombian and Isthmian work favours small lost-wax casts with 'false filigree'.
techniques.blurb: Gold was the first metal of the Americas and metallurgy moved south to north: Peru, then Colombia, then the Isthmus, then Mexico. Andean smiths valued colour over purity and invented surface-enrichment gilding to make copper-rich alloys look like gold.

techniques.name: Platinum

arrivals.note: recognised as a new metal
workable in quantity only from c. 1790-1805
'garland style' diamond settings, c. 1895-1940

techniques.rule: Platinum-set jewellery outside pre-Columbian Ecuador/Colombia ⇒ after c. 1790, and in practice c. 1895 or later (final era). White-metal diamond jewellery before that is silver, usually tarnished grey.
techniques.lookFor: Bright grey-white metal that does not tarnish, used in very fine, lace-like diamond mounts; silver settings look darker and bulkier. La Tolita pieces are tiny gold objects with whitish platinum-rich patches.
techniques.blurb: Smiths at La Tolita sintered platinum grains with gold two thousand years before Europe could melt the metal. In the Old World it is effectively a 19th-20th century material, which makes it a clean terminus post quem.

techniques.name: Garnet cloisonne (Migration Period polychrome style)

arrivals.note: eagle brooches

end.note: garnet supply from India/Sri Lanka dries up and the fashion ends by c. 700

techniques.rule: Gold jewellery or sword fittings covered in flat red garnets in gold cells ⇒ c. 375-700 CE (eras 250-500 and 500-750), in Europe or the Pontic steppe.
techniques.lookFor: A mosaic of thin, flat-cut dark red stones in a honeycomb of gold walls, often over patterned gold foil that glitters through; shapes include eagles, cicadas, stepped and mushroom cells. No coloured glass enamel.
techniques.blurb: The style travelled west with the peoples of the Migration Period, from Hunnic-era workshops around the Black Sea to Frankish, Visigothic and Anglo-Saxon courts. It is one of the tightest date ranges in early medieval metalwork.

techniques.name: Spoke-wheeled horse chariot

arrivals.note: earlier Sinauli cart/chariot finds (c. 1900 BCE) are debated

end.note: war chariots replaced by cavalry across most of Eurasia between c. 500 and 300 BCE; survive for racing and ceremony

techniques.rule: Light two-wheeled spoked chariot depicted ⇒ not before c. 2000 BCE anywhere, c. 1600 BCE in Egypt (so not Old or Middle Kingdom), c. 1200 BCE in China. Solid-wheeled ass-drawn battle wagons are earlier (Sumer, c. 2600 BCE).
techniques.lookFor: Count the spokes and check the animal: 4-spoke wheels are early (Egypt 18th Dynasty, Mycenae), 6-8 spokes later; Chinese chariots have many (18-30) spokes. Horses, not onagers or oxen, with a standing driver.
techniques.blurb: The chariot package (domestic horse, spoked wheel, bit) spread from the steppe across Eurasia in about 800 years. In Egypt it is a marker of the New Kingdom; in China of the late Shang.

techniques.name: Paired stirrups

arrivals.note: toe-ring only; not a true stirrup

techniques.rule: Rider with stirrups ⇒ not before c. 300 CE in China, c. 600 in Byzantium/Europe, c. 700 in the Islamic world. Greek, Roman, Achaemenid, Parthian, Sasanian, Han and Scythian riders have legs hanging free. Tang horse figures usually show stirrups; Han ones never do.
techniques.lookFor: Look under the rider's foot or hanging from the saddle of a riderless horse: a loop or flat-bottomed ring on a strap. Absence of stirrups with dangling toes pointing down signals antiquity.
techniques.blurb: A single mounting stirrup appears on a Chinese tomb figure dated 302 CE and a pair on one dated 322. The Avars carried the idea to Europe in the late 6th century.

techniques.name: Full steel plate armour

arrivals.note: Gothic then fluted 'Maximilian' armour c. 1500-1530
influenced by European cuirasses and firearms

end.note: firearms make full harness obsolete; cuirass and helmet linger for cavalry

techniques.rule: Complete articulated steel harness (cap-a-pie) ⇒ c. 1400-1650 (eras 1250-1500 or 1500-1750). Etched and gilded parade armour ⇒ after c. 1500. Mail hauberk with only a few plates ⇒ 1250-1400; mail alone with nasal helmet ⇒ 900-1250.
techniques.lookFor: Smooth polished steel covering the whole body with overlapping lames at joints, a closed helmet (armet, sallet, close helm) and a breastplate; fluting = German c. 1500-1530; peascod belly = c. 1570-1600.
techniques.blurb: The knight in shining armour is late: full plate matures only around 1400-1420 and is gone as battlefield equipment by the mid-17th century. Bronze muscle cuirasses of Greece and Rome are a different, much older thing.

techniques.name: Japanese curved sword (tachi, katana)

arrivals.note: uchigatana/katana replace tachi during the Muromachi period
standard samurai wear in the Edo period

end.note: Haitorei edict bans wearing swords; fittings makers turn to export art metalwork

techniques.rule: Curved single-edged Japanese blade ⇒ after c. 900 CE (straight chokuto before, Kofun-Nara). Katana mounting with tsuba and wrapped hilt thrust through the belt ⇒ after c. 1400. Elaborate soft-metal tsuba, kozuka and menuki as art objects ⇒ mostly Edo 1600-1868.
techniques.lookFor: Gentle curve, ridge line (shinogi), wavy temper line (hamon) along the edge, long tang with file marks and a peg hole; tachi hang edge-down from cords, katana sit edge-up in the sash.
techniques.blurb: Japanese smiths moved from straight continental-style blades to the curved, differentially hardened tachi in the mid-Heian period. Most sword fittings in museums are Edo-period luxury craft rather than battlefield gear.

techniques.name: Gunpowder firearms

arrivals.note: first European depiction of a cannon
Deccan sultanates first; field artillery and matchlocks with Babur, 1526

techniques.rule: Any gun or cannon depicted or present ⇒ after c. 1290 (China), c. 1330 (Europe/Islamic lands), 1543 (Japan), 1492+ (Americas). Matchlock (S-shaped serpentine, smouldering cord) ⇒ c. 1470+; wheellock ⇒ c. 1510+; flintlock ⇒ c. 1610+; percussion cap ⇒ c. 1820+; metallic cartridge revolver/breech-loader ⇒ c. 1855+.
techniques.lookFor: Check the lock: a curved arm holding cord (matchlock), a steel wheel and key square (wheellock), a cock gripping a flint with an L-shaped frizzen (flintlock), a small hammer and nipple (percussion). Powder flasks and bandoliers date the same way.
techniques.blurb: Gunpowder is a 9th-century Chinese discovery, metal-barrelled guns a late 13th-century one. The lock mechanism is one of the most reliable datable details in any picture or object.

techniques.name: Jomon cord-marked pottery

arrivals.note: flamboyant rims c. 3000-2000 BCE
goggle-eyed dogu c. 1000-400 BCE

end.note: replaced by plainer, wheel-finished Yayoi pottery with wet-rice farming (start now often put nearer 900-400 BCE in Kyushu)

techniques.rule: Japanese hand-built pot with rolled-cord texture ⇒ before c. 300 BCE. Flame-rim vessels ⇒ era 3000-2000 BCE. Goggle-eyed dogu ⇒ c. 1000-400 BCE. Smooth reddish thin-walled jars ⇒ Yayoi (300 BCE-300 CE); grey wheel-thrown stoneware ⇒ Sue ware, after c. 400 CE.
techniques.lookFor: Low-fired brown/black earthenware, coil-built, surfaces impressed with twisted cord in herringbone bands; exuberant sculpted rims with loops and crests. No glaze, no wheel lines, no paint beyond occasional red.
techniques.blurb: Among the oldest pottery in the world, made by sedentary hunter-gatherers for over ten thousand years. The name itself means 'cord-marked'.

techniques.name: Potter's wheel

arrivals.note: thin black 'eggshell' wares; probably independent
with Greek and Phoenician colonists
all pre-Columbian pottery is hand-built or mould-made

techniques.rule: Wheel-thrown pot (spiral throwing ridges, perfect symmetry, string-cut base) ⇒ not pre-Columbian American, and not traditional sub-Saharan African or Oceanian. In temperate Europe ⇒ after c. 500 BCE; in Britain ⇒ after c. 100 BCE; in Japan ⇒ after c. 400 CE.
techniques.lookFor: Fine parallel horizontal ridges inside and out, thin even walls, true circular rims, concentric cut marks under the foot. Hand-built pots show slight asymmetry, coil joins, scraped or burnished surfaces, and rounded bases.
techniques.blurb: The fast wheel is a marker of urban, specialist production. Its total absence in the Americas before 1492 is one of the most useful single facts for the game: Moche, Maya, Nazca and Pueblo vessels were all coiled, paddled or moulded.

techniques.name: Egyptian faience

arrivals.note: 'snake goddess' figures

end.note: production dwindles in the Roman period; replaced by true glazed pottery and glass

techniques.rule: Bright turquoise-blue glazed quartz-paste object (shabti, amulet, bead net, hippo, chalice) ⇒ Egypt or its sphere, c. 3000 BCE-300 CE. Mass-produced shabti figures ⇒ New Kingdom to Ptolemaic (c. 1500-30 BCE); large sets of small pale-green shabtis ⇒ Late Period (after c. 700 BCE).
techniques.lookFor: Matte-to-glassy turquoise, blue or green surface over a gritty white core visible at chips; details painted in black-purple manganese. It is not clay and usually small; forms are moulded, not thrown.
techniques.blurb: Not true faience at all but a self-glazing quartz ceramic, the first high-tech synthetic material. Its blue stood in for turquoise and lapis, and it was traded as beads from Britain to the Indus.

techniques.name: Greek black-figure pottery

arrivals.note: dominates the market from c. 570 BCE

end.note: superseded by red-figure; survives only on Panathenaic prize amphorae into the 2nd c. BCE

techniques.rule: Black silhouette figures with incised details on orange clay ⇒ c. 700-480 BCE (era 750-500 BCE). Earlier: Geometric pottery with meanders and stick figures (900-700 BCE). Small Corinthian aryballoi with friezes of animals and rosettes ⇒ 650-550 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: Figures are solid glossy black with details scratched through to the clay; women's skin in added white, some purple-red. Background is the bare orange clay.
techniques.blurb: Invented at Corinth and perfected at Athens (Exekias, c. 540 BCE), black-figure is the signature of Archaic Greece. Most surviving examples come from Etruscan tombs.

techniques.name: Greek red-figure pottery

arrivals.note: Greek colonial workshops; big ornate funerary vases

end.note: Athenian production ends c. 320 BCE and South Italian soon after; plain black-gloss and moulded wares follow

techniques.rule: Reserved orange figures on black ground ⇒ c. 525-300 BCE (eras 750-500 BCE at the very end, mostly 500-250 BCE). Huge volute kraters crammed with figures, white and yellow added paint ⇒ Apulia c. 370-300 BCE. White-ground lekythoi ⇒ Athens c. 470-400 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: The background is painted black and the figures left in clay colour, with details drawn in fine black lines (not incised). Anatomy becomes more naturalistic, with three-quarter views and drapery folds.
techniques.blurb: The reversal of black-figure around 530-520 BCE let painters draw rather than engrave. After Athens lost the western market in the Peloponnesian War, Greek potters in southern Italy took over until about 300 BCE.

techniques.name: Terra sigillata (Roman red-gloss tableware)

arrivals.note: Hellenistic red-gloss forerunner
dominates Mediterranean trade to the 7th c.

end.note: African Red Slip, the last major branch, ends in the 7th century

techniques.rule: Glossy brick-red moulded or stamped tableware ⇒ Roman world, c. 50 BCE-650 CE; Gaulish 'samian' with moulded hunt scenes and name stamps ⇒ c. 20-250 CE (era 0-250). Greek-style black-gloss tableware is the predecessor (before c. 50 BCE).
techniques.lookFor: Uniform sealing-wax red, semi-glossy slip on fine clay; standard plates and bowls with crisp profiles, moulded relief friezes, and a rectangular potter's stamp in the centre of the floor.
techniques.blurb: Rome's switch from black to red tableware around 40 BCE is a tidy chronological hinge. Standardised forms and potters' stamps make sigillata the archaeologist's favourite dating tool.

techniques.name: Lead-glazed earthenware

arrivals.note: Warring States beginnings; common on Han tomb models
no true glazes in the pre-Columbian Americas

techniques.rule: Glassy glazed pottery ⇒ not before c. 100 BCE in Europe or China (alkaline-glazed Near Eastern and faience wares excepted), essentially absent in Europe 400-850 CE outside Byzantium, and not pre-Columbian American (Plumbate and Pueblo 'glaze-paint' are special cases). Green-glazed Han watchtowers, granaries and hill jars ⇒ China c. 100 BCE-220 CE.
techniques.lookFor: Shiny, transparent, often crazed coating in honey-yellow, green (copper) or brown (iron) that pools in hollows and runs; Han glazes often turn silvery-iridescent from burial.
techniques.blurb: Lead makes glaze melt at earthenware temperatures. Roman and Han potters adopted it around the same time, apparently independently; in Europe it becomes universal only in the Middle Ages.

techniques.name: Celadon (green-glazed stoneware)

arrivals.note: exported; inspires local imitations
inlaid sanggam celadon from c. 1150
thick jade-like glaze; mass export 1200-1450

techniques.rule: Grey-green glazed stoneware ⇒ China after c. 150 CE (proto-celadons earlier); Korean celadon ⇒ c. 950-1400 (era 750-1000 end, 1000-1250, 1250-1500), with black-and-white inlay under the glaze ⇒ after c. 1150. Thai celadon ⇒ c. 1350-1550.
techniques.lookFor: Soft sea-green to olive translucent glaze over grey stoneware, pooling darker in carved or combed lines; Goryeo pieces have inlaid white and black cranes, clouds and chrysanthemums; Longquan has a thick, bluish-green unctuous glaze, often with unglazed orange-burnt biscuit details.
techniques.blurb: Celadon imitates jade. It was the world's most traded ceramic before blue-and-white, turning up from Japan to Cairo and Kilwa, and Korea's Goryeo potters made what many Chinese connoisseurs judged the best of all.

techniques.name: Tang sancai (three-colour lead glaze) & tomb figures

arrivals.note: inspired by Chinese imports
Liao sancai revival, 10th-11th c.

end.note: tomb sancai collapses after the An Lushan rebellion (755-763)

techniques.rule: Camel, horse, groom, court lady or guardian figure with dripping amber-green-cream glaze ⇒ Tang China c. 680-760 (era 500-750 or 750-1000 boundary; guess c. 700-750). Unglazed painted grey figures ⇒ Han to Sui (206 BCE-618 CE). Green-glazed Han models are monochrome.
techniques.lookFor: White earthenware body with runny splashes of amber, green and cream (rarely blue); faces of figures often left unglazed and cold-painted. Plump court ladies, bearded foreign grooms, Bactrian camels with musicians.
techniques.blurb: Sancai was largely funerary ware for the Tang aristocracy, made for barely a century. The Central Asian merchants and two-humped camels it depicts are the Silk Road in clay.

techniques.name: True porcelain

arrivals.note: qingbai; imperial kilns from the Ming
white porcelain dominant under Joseon from the 15th c.
experimental, c. 1575-1587
exported by the Dutch as Imari and Kakiemon c. 1650-1750
Bottger's success 1708; factory 1710

techniques.rule: White translucent porcelain ⇒ China only before c. 1000; Korea/Vietnam after that; Japan only after 1616; Europe only after 1710 (bar rare Medici pieces), so European porcelain figures and tea services ⇒ 1710+ (mostly era 1750-2000). Persian and Ottoman 'porcelain-look' wares are fritware.
techniques.lookFor: Pure white, thin, glassy, slightly translucent body that chips with a shell-like fracture; rings when struck. Earthenware imitations (tin-glaze, fritware) show a buff or grainy body at chips and foot rings.
techniques.blurb: Porcelain needs kaolin, china stone and 1300 C kilns. China kept the secret for a millennium; Europeans called it 'white gold' and only cracked it in Saxony in 1708.

techniques.name: Underglaze cobalt blue-and-white

arrivals.note: tin-glazed, inspired by Manila galleon imports

techniques.rule: Blue-and-white porcelain ⇒ after c. 1320 (never Song or Tang in practice). Outside China ⇒ after c. 1400; in Japan ⇒ after 1616; European blue-and-white ⇒ tin-glaze from c. 1620, porcelain from c. 1720. Kraak panels (radiating rim panels) ⇒ Chinese export c. 1570-1640.
techniques.lookFor: Cobalt-blue painting under a clear glaze on white. Yuan/early Ming: dark, 'heaped and piled' blue with dense bands; Kangxi (1662-1722): bright sapphire washes; Delft: softer blue on a thicker, chipping white tin glaze over buff clay.
techniques.blurb: Persian cobalt met Chinese porcelain under the Mongols; the dated David Vases (1351) show the style fully formed. For the next 400 years most of the world's potters tried to copy it.

techniques.name: Qing overglaze enamels (famille verte, famille rose)

arrivals.note: Japanese overglaze enamel begins slightly earlier
opaque pink from colloidal gold, technique from Europe

techniques.rule: Opaque pink/rose enamel on Chinese porcelain ⇒ after c. 1720 (so era 1500-1750's last decades or 1750-2000). Translucent green-dominated enamels with iron red and no pink ⇒ Kangxi famille verte c. 1680-1725. Ming enamels (wucai, doucai) use underglaze blue with red, green, yellow, c. 1465-1640.
techniques.lookFor: Famille verte: clear emerald greens, iron red, yellow, aubergine, over-glaze blue, flat and translucent. Famille rose: soft opaque pinks and whites allowing shading, pastel palette, often dense floral or figure scenes with gilding.
techniques.blurb: The pink came from the same gold-ruby technology European enamellers used; Jesuits brought it to the Kangxi court around 1720. It instantly made the older green palette look old-fashioned.

techniques.name: Tin-glazed earthenware (maiolica, faience, delftware)

arrivals.note: Malaga then Valencia (Manises), 13th-15th c.
istoriato narrative painting c. 1500-1570

end.note: cheaper, tougher creamware and porcelain displace tin-glaze in Europe c. 1770-1800

techniques.rule: Opaque white-glazed painted earthenware ⇒ after c. 800 CE in the Islamic world; Spain after c. 1000; Italy after c. 1250 (polychrome Renaissance maiolica ⇒ 1450-1600); Northern Europe ⇒ after c. 1510, mostly 1600-1780. Not Roman, not early medieval European.
techniques.lookFor: Thick, soft, opaque white glaze that chips to reveal buff/pink clay; colours painted on top sink in slightly (cobalt blue, copper green, manganese purple, antimony yellow, orange). Italian istoriato covers the whole dish with a narrative scene.
techniques.blurb: Abbasid potters added tin oxide to glaze to imitate Chinese white wares. The idea then walked west and north for 800 years: Baghdad, Cairo, Malaga, Mallorca (hence 'maiolica'), Faenza (hence 'faience'), Antwerp and Delft.

techniques.name: Lustreware

arrivals.note: star-and-cross tiles, c. 1200-1340
Hispano-Moresque gold lustre, peak 1400-1500

arrivals.place: England (Staffordshire pink and silver lustre; De Morgan)

techniques.rule: Metallic gold/copper sheen painted on a white glaze ⇒ after c. 850 CE and Islamic until c. 1500; Spanish armorial lustre dishes ⇒ c. 1400-1550; Italian lustred maiolica ⇒ c. 1500-1550. Kashan lustre tiles ⇒ c. 1200-1340.
techniques.lookFor: A thin iridescent film, brassy yellow to coppery red, shifting with the light, over an opaque white (tin or frit) glaze. Fatimid: bold figures; Kashan: figures reserved in a lustre ground with tiny spirals; Manises: ivy and bryony leaves, shields, blue plus gold.
techniques.blurb: Lustre is a second, smoky firing that leaves a nanolayer of silver and copper on the glaze, a technique borrowed from glass painters. Workshops moved as dynasties fell: Iraq to Fatimid Cairo, to Syria and Kashan, to Spain.

techniques.name: Iznik ware

arrivals.place: Istanbul (tile revetments in mosques and Topkapi)

arrivals.note: smaller-scale successor, 18th c.

end.note: quality declines after c. 1620 and Iznik production ends around 1700

techniques.rule: Fritware with raised tomato-red, cobalt and turquoise tulips and carnations ⇒ Ottoman c. 1557-1650 (era 1500-1750). Blue-and-white only with tight arabesques ⇒ c. 1480-1520. Sage green and manganese purple ('Damascus' palette) ⇒ c. 1540-1555.
techniques.lookFor: Brilliant white ground, glassy clear glaze, black outlines, and a thick sealing-wax red standing in relief; saz leaves, tulips, carnations, hyacinths, ships; rims with 'rock and wave' border copied from Chinese porcelain.
techniques.blurb: Ottoman court designers and Iznik potters created a new palette almost decade by decade, which makes Iznik unusually easy to date. The relief red appears with the Suleymaniye mosque in the late 1550s.

techniques.name: Transfer-printed ceramics

arrivals.place: United States (imported Staffordshire views, then local)

techniques.rule: Printed (not hand-painted) decoration on pottery ⇒ after 1752, and blue transfer-printed earthenware ⇒ after c. 1784: firmly the 1750-2000 era. Creamware and white 'pearlware' bodies likewise ⇒ after c. 1760.
techniques.lookFor: Engraved-line look: shading made of dots and hatching, identical repeat on every piece, seams or misalignments where tissue sheets met, usually one colour (blue, black, brown, later pink/green).
techniques.blurb: Printing from engraved copper plates onto pots let Staffordshire flood the world with cheap decorated tableware. With Wedgwood's creamware (1760s) and jasperware (1775) it marks the industrial end of the ceramics story.

techniques.name: Stirrup-spout vessels (Cupisnique, Moche, Chimu)

arrivals.note: a possible early link with Ecuador
portrait heads and fineline painting, c. 100-800 CE
c. 900-1470, continuing under the Inca

end.note: form dies out in the early colonial period

techniques.rule: Bottle with a hollow loop handle and single spout ⇒ north coast of Peru (or Ecuador). Thick grey/black incised, heavy spout with flanged lip ⇒ Cupisnique/Chavin c. 1200-200 BCE. Cream-and-red realistic portrait heads, warriors, animals ⇒ Moche c. 100-800 CE. Glossy black mould-made with a small monkey at the spout join ⇒ Chimu c. 1000-1470.
techniques.lookFor: The stirrup: two arched tubes joining into one vertical spout. Moche = bichrome red on cream, sculptural realism, fineline scenes; Chimu = uniform shiny black, pressed relief, stippled backgrounds.
techniques.blurb: One vessel shape persisted on the north coast for nearly three thousand years, so the spout profile and surface colour do the dating. Nazca and the southern Andes preferred the double-spout-and-bridge bottle instead.

techniques.name: Maya polychrome pottery

arrivals.note: black line on cream, c. 675-750

end.note: painted cylinder-vase tradition ends with the Classic Maya collapse; Postclassic wares are plumbate, fine orange and effigy censers

techniques.rule: Cylinder vase or plate painted in orange, red and black with courtly scenes and a glyph band under the rim ⇒ Classic Maya, c. 250-900 CE and mostly 600-850 (eras 500-750, 750-1000). Shiny grey-olive hard 'Plumbate' effigy jars ⇒ c. 900-1100.
techniques.lookFor: Slip-painted (not glazed), glossy from burnishing; straight-walled cylinders, tripod plates; figures in profile with elaborate headdresses, speech scrolls; a rim text of glyph blocks (the dedicatory formula naming the vessel as a cacao cup).
techniques.blurb: The vases were chocolate cups for the nobility, signed and inscribed. Because almost all of them fall inside the Late Classic, a painted Maya cylinder is one of the safer era guesses in Mesoamerica.

techniques.name: Pueblo & Mimbres painted pottery

arrivals.note: figurative bowls c. 1000-1150
yellow ware with free, asymmetric designs

arrivals.place: Hopi & San Ildefonso revivals (Nampeyo, Maria Martinez)
arrivals.note: art-pottery revivals; black-on-black from 1919

techniques.rule: Black geometric paint on white slip from the US Southwest ⇒ c. 600-1300 CE. Bowl interior with a single stylised animal or figure and a 'kill hole' ⇒ Mimbres c. 1000-1150 (era 1000-1250). Polychrome on yellow/buff ⇒ after c. 1300. Signed, highly polished blackware ⇒ 20th century.
techniques.lookFor: Coil-built, thin, white-slipped with crisp black hatching, steps, spirals and interlocking frets; hemispherical bowls, ollas, mugs, ladles. No glaze, no wheel marks.
techniques.blurb: Southwestern pottery is tree-ring dated to within decades, and black-on-white collapses with the great migrations around 1300. Mimbres figurative bowls, found inverted over the heads of the dead, come from little more than a century.

techniques.name: Core-formed glass vessels

arrivals.note: peak under Amenhotep III and Akhenaten

arrivals.place: Mycenaean Greece (moulded glass beads and inlays)

arrivals.note: small alabastra, amphoriskoi, traded everywhere to c. 50 BCE

end.note: made obsolete by glassblowing

techniques.rule: Small opaque dark-blue bottle with yellow/white/turquoise zigzag trails ⇒ c. 1500-1100 BCE (Egypt/Mesopotamia) or c. 550-50 BCE (Mediterranean). No glass vessels at all before c. 1550 BCE; glass essentially vanishes c. 1100-800 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: Tiny (5-15 cm), thick-walled, opaque, with combed feather or zigzag trails dragged into the surface; rough interior; applied handles and rim. Shapes copy Greek pots (alabastron, amphoriskos, oinochoe) in the later group, Egyptian palm-column kohl tubes and krateriskoi in the earlier.
techniques.blurb: Before blowing, vessels were built by winding hot glass around a clay-dung core on a rod. Glass was a palace luxury on a par with lapis and turquoise, which it imitated.

techniques.name: Mosaic & millefiori glass

arrivals.note: fused mosaic bowls, network and gold-band glass
ribbon and millefiori bowls, late 1st c. BCE-1st c. CE
revived; 'millefiori' beads and paperweights from the 1830s-40s

techniques.rule: Shallow bowl fused from slices of multicoloured canes ⇒ Hellenistic-early Roman, c. 250 BCE-100 CE (eras 250-0 BCE, 0-250 CE). Glass paperweights with flower canes ⇒ after 1845. Millefiori trade beads in African jewellery ⇒ c. 1850-1950.
techniques.lookFor: A patchwork of little flower, spiral or star cross-sections embedded edge-to-edge; ancient bowls are open, polished forms with a twisted cane rim, usually in purple, white, yellow, green.
techniques.blurb: Bundled coloured rods are stretched into canes, sliced, and fused over a mould. Roman glassmakers dropped the technique once blowing made cheap vessels possible, and Venice rediscovered it fifteen centuries later.

techniques.name: Glassblowing

arrivals.note: thick facet-cut bowls traded east to China and Japan
blowing introduced in the 5th c.; glass stays a minor art until the Qing
regular production only after European contact

techniques.rule: Blown glass ⇒ not before c. 50 BCE. Thin-walled transparent vessels, mould-blown bottles, or anything with a pontil scar ⇒ Roman period or later. In China, glass vessels of any date are rare; elaborate Chinese glass ⇒ Qing (after c. 1700).
techniques.lookFor: Thin, light, symmetrical walls, bubbles stretched in one direction, a rough pontil scar on the base, folded rims, pinched or trailed decoration; pale blue-green natural tint and rainbow weathering on Roman pieces. Earlier glass is small, thick, opaque (core-formed) or cast and wheel-polished.
techniques.blurb: The blowpipe turned glass from a jewel into a household material within two generations of its invention in the Levant, just as Rome absorbed the region. Square mould-blown bottles and little unguent flasks are the commonest Roman finds.

techniques.name: Cameo glass

arrivals.note: 9th-10th c. cameo and relief cutting
especially snuff bottles

end.note: Roman cameo glass is confined to c. 30 BCE-60 CE, with a small revival in the late 3rd-4th c.

techniques.rule: White-on-dark-blue carved glass with classical figures ⇒ early Imperial Rome (c. 30 BCE-60 CE) or a Victorian revival (1876-1910). Multi-layer coloured overlay on Chinese snuff bottles or vases ⇒ 1700-1900. Floral acid-etched cameo vases ⇒ Art Nouveau, 1885-1914.
techniques.lookFor: Two (or more) fused layers of differently coloured glass, the upper cut away to leave a relief design, like a hardstone cameo. Roman: opaque white on cobalt; Galle: organic colours with plants and insects, often signed.
techniques.blurb: The Portland Vase is the type specimen; Wedgwood copied it in jasperware (1790) and Northwood in glass (1876). The Roman output was a short Augustan fashion, which is why the date range is so tight.

techniques.name: Enamelled & gilded Islamic glass (Mamluk mosque lamps)

arrivals.note: Mamluk mosque lamps peak c. 1300-1380
'Aldrevandin' group c. 1300; major revival c. 1460

arrivals.place: Mughal India (gilded and enamelled glass huqqa bases)

end.note: Syrian workshops ruined by Timur's sack of Damascus (1400-01); later Mamluk lamps were ordered from Venice

techniques.rule: Glass lamp, beaker or bottle with red-outlined gilding, blue enamel and bold Arabic inscription bands ⇒ Syria/Egypt c. 1200-1400 (eras 1000-1250 end, 1250-1500). Enamelled glass with European coats of arms ⇒ Venice after c. 1460 or Germany after 1570.
techniques.lookFor: Honey-tinted bubbly glass, vase-shaped lamp with flaring neck and suspension loops; thick blue, red, white enamels and gold; thuluth inscriptions and round heraldic blazons (cup, napkin, sword).
techniques.blurb: Ayyubid and Mamluk glassmakers were the first to fire coloured enamels and gold onto glass at scale. Venice learned the trick and, after 1400, sold it back to the Islamic world.

techniques.name: Venetian cristallo & facon de Venise

end.note: fashion shifts to heavy English lead glass and Bohemian engraved crystal

techniques.rule: Colourless, paper-thin goblets with fantastical stems, filigree (white-thread 'latticino') or ice-glass ⇒ Venice or facon de Venise, c. 1450-1700 (eras 1250-1500 end, 1500-1750). Filigrana canes ⇒ after 1527. Before 1450 European glass is greenish forest glass.
techniques.lookFor: Very thin, slightly greyish clear glass, tall winged or serpent stems, applied blue pincered trails, white twisted-thread patterns in the wall; light and delicate, never deeply cut.
techniques.blurb: Angelo Barovier's decolourised cristallo made Venice the supplier of Renaissance Europe's table glass, and emigrant Muranese workers spread the style despite the Republic's bans.

techniques.name: Lead crystal & cut glass

arrivals.note: parallel non-lead crystal for deep engraving

techniques.rule: Heavy, brilliantly clear, deeply cut or wheel-engraved glass ⇒ after c. 1680 (era 1500-1750 tail, mostly 1750-2000). English baluster and air-twist stem wine glasses ⇒ c. 1690-1780. Machine-pressed patterned glass ⇒ after 1825.
techniques.lookFor: Thick walls, strong sparkle and prismatic fire, sharp diamond and star cutting, a ground-out pontil; engraved Bohemian pieces show matte pictorial scenes and coats of arms.
techniques.blurb: Ravenscroft's lead glass (patent 1674) was soft enough to cut and refractive enough to flash like rock crystal, ending Venice's dominance. Bohemia reached a similar result with chalk and potash.

techniques.name: Stained-glass windows

arrivals.note: lets one pane be white and yellow

arrivals.place: United States (Tiffany, La Farge opalescent glass)

techniques.rule: Leaded figural window panel ⇒ after c. 1100 (coloured window glass fragments exist from the 7th-9th c.). Deep blue-and-ruby mosaic style ⇒ 1140-1260; yellow silver-stain and large clear areas ⇒ after c. 1310; painterly enamel on clear panes ⇒ after c. 1520; streaky opalescent glass with no painting ⇒ USA after 1880.
techniques.lookFor: Pieces of coloured glass held in H-section lead cames, details in dark brown vitreous paint; medieval figures under canopies with Lombardic or blackletter text.
techniques.blurb: The oldest complete windows still in place are the late 11th-century prophets at Augsburg. The art rose with Gothic architecture, nearly died in the Reformation, and was mass-produced again in the 19th century.

techniques.name: Silk & sericulture

arrivals.note: wild Antheraea silk, independent of China
silk arrives as cloth and yarn; no local silkworms
silkworm eggs smuggled under Justinian
Palermo royal workshop 1147; Lucca, Venice, Florence, Genoa by 1300
Huguenot weavers

techniques.rule: Woven silk made in the Mediterranean ⇒ after 553 CE; made in Italy ⇒ after c. 1150; in France ⇒ after c. 1470; in England ⇒ after c. 1685. Silk fabric found west of Central Asia before c. 100 BCE is very unlikely.
techniques.lookFor: Smooth, lustrous, very fine threads with sharp pattern definition and saturated dyes; complex figured weaves (damask, samite, lampas, brocade). Wool is matte and fuzzy, linen is stiff and undyed-looking, cotton is matte and printed or painted.
techniques.blurb: China kept sericulture to itself for some three thousand years. The Byzantine industry started with eggs hidden in monks' canes, and each later European centre was seeded by migrant weavers from the last.

techniques.name: Cotton

arrivals.note: separate species; indigo-dyed cotton c. 4000 BCE
becomes the common cloth under the Yuan and Ming

techniques.rule: Cotton cloth in Europe ⇒ essentially after c. 950 (Mediterranean) and common in northern Europe only after c. 1600; in China common only after c. 1250; in West Africa after c. 1000. Ancient Egyptian textiles are linen; ancient Near Eastern and European are wool and linen. Andean and Indian cotton can be any date.
techniques.lookFor: Matte, soft, slightly fuzzy plain weave that takes paint, resist and print well (unlike wool, which is tapestry-woven or embroidered, and linen, which is usually left pale).
techniques.blurb: Cotton was domesticated at least four times, twice in the Old World and twice in the New. Until the Islamic expansion carried it west it was a South Asian speciality, which is why Indian printed cottons were such a shock to Europe.

techniques.name: Andean camelid-fibre tapestry & embroidery

arrivals.note: Necropolis mantles c. 300 BCE-200 CE
abstract staff-bearer figures, four-cornered hats, c. 600-1000

arrivals.place: Colonial Andes (tapestry with European motifs, silk and metal thread)

techniques.rule: Flying figures embroidered in stem stitch on dark ground ⇒ Paracas c. 300 BCE-200 CE. Tapestry tunic with compressed, abstract profile faces in strict columns ⇒ Wari c. 600-1000 (eras 500-750, 750-1000). Small square geometric tocapu blocks or checkerboard tunic ⇒ Inca 1450-1532. Lions, crowns, double-headed eagles, silk ⇒ colonial, after 1532.
techniques.lookFor: Brilliantly dyed alpaca/vicuna weft over cotton warp, extremely fine tapestry (often 60-100+ wefts per cm), saturated reds from cochineal, blues from indigo; tunics are sleeveless rectangles with a neck slit.
techniques.blurb: In the Andes cloth outranked gold; the dry coast preserved it in quantity. Because each culture had a very different textile grammar, textiles are often easier to date than Andean metal.

techniques.name: Knotted-pile carpets

origin.place: Altai / West or Central Asia (Pazyryk carpet)

arrivals.note: 'Holbein', 'Lotto', 'Bellini' patterns datable by paintings, c. 1450-1650
medallion and garden carpets; Ardabil carpet dated 1539-40

techniques.rule: Surviving whole pile carpets ⇒ almost never before c. 1250 and overwhelmingly after 1450. Persian curvilinear medallion carpets ⇒ after c. 1500; Mughal flower-lattice carpets ⇒ after c. 1620; European hand-knotted carpets ⇒ after c. 1620. Harsh orange/magenta in a rug ⇒ synthetic dyes, after c. 1870.
techniques.lookFor: Tufts of wool or silk knotted in rows giving a velvety surface; look at borders and field: angular geometric repeat (Anatolian, Caucasian, Turkmen), curvilinear scrolls with central medallion (Persian), naturalistic flowers on red (Mughal).
techniques.blurb: The frozen Pazyryk carpet of the 5th-4th century BCE is already technically mature, but almost nothing else survives until Seljuk Anatolia. Europeans loved Turkish rugs so much that pattern types are named after the painters who depicted them.

techniques.name: Ikat (resist-dyed yarn)

arrivals.note: Asuka-period warp ikat banners, probably continental
exported to Southeast Asia as heirlooms
certainly older; surviving cloths are mostly 19th-20th c.
bold silk ikat robes, c. 1800-1900

techniques.rule: Ikat's origin is undatable, so use the regional window: Yemeni inscribed cotton ikat ⇒ 9th-10th c.; Central Asian silk ikat coats ⇒ 1800-1920; Japanese indigo kasuri ⇒ after c. 1600 (mostly 1750+); Indonesian examples in museums ⇒ nearly all 1800-1950.
techniques.lookFor: Motifs have characteristic feathered, blurry edges along the thread direction because the yarn was tie-dyed before weaving. Bukhara ikats: huge cloud-like motifs in clashing colours on silk; patola: crisp double-ikat grids with elephants and flowers.
techniques.blurb: The technique was probably invented several times; the word is Malay. Ajanta murals suggest it in India by the 5th-7th century, but because cloth rots the surviving record starts late and is dominated by the 19th century.

techniques.name: Batik (wax-resist dyeing)

arrivals.note: wax-resist linen mummy wrappings; Tang China and Nara Japan also used wax resist
Nara-period wax-resist silks
court styles of Yogyakarta and Surakarta

techniques.rule: Fine Javanese batik on machine-smooth cotton ⇒ in practice after c. 1750 (most museum pieces 1850-1950). Stamped (cap) batik ⇒ after c. 1840. 'African wax print' cloth ⇒ after c. 1890. Aniline-bright pinks and greens ⇒ after c. 1870.
techniques.lookFor: Pattern reserved in pale lines or dots against indigo blue and soga brown; hairline 'crackle' veins where dye entered cracks in the wax; design identical on both faces. Court motifs: parang diagonal knives, kawung circles.
techniques.blurb: Wax resist is ancient and widespread, but the Javanese art using the spouted canting pen is documented only from the 17th century onward, and its date of origin is argued. Dutch factories copied it for Java, failed, and found their market in West Africa instead.

techniques.name: Velvet

arrivals.note: major producer, exporting to Venice
earliest surviving velvets; Italian industry dominant c. 1350-1600
large carnation and ogival lattices in crimson and gold

techniques.rule: Surviving silk velvet ⇒ after c. 1250-1300 in practice (texts mention it in Abbasid Baghdad c. 800); voided and gold-brocaded 'pomegranate' velvets ⇒ Italy/Spain c. 1420-1550 (era 1250-1500 or 1500-1750); Ottoman catma ⇒ c. 1470-1700. Not Roman, not early medieval, not Tang.
techniques.lookFor: Dense short pile that looks darker or lighter with the light; 'voided' velvets leave flat satin ground showing the pattern; gold loops (boucle) in the richest. Large artichoke/pomegranate motifs on curving stems are the 15th-century signature, visible in portraits too.
techniques.blurb: Velvet needs an extra pile warp and a complex loom. Texts place it in Abbasid Baghdad and Mamluk Cairo, but the surviving record begins with the mature Italian silk industry around 1300. Renaissance Italy and Ottoman Bursa traded designs so closely that their velvets can be hard to tell apart.

techniques.name: Lace (needle and bobbin)
techniques.rule: True lace on an object or in a portrait ⇒ after c. 1520, and realistically 1550+. Starched ruff ⇒ c. 1560-1630; flat falling lace collar ⇒ c. 1620-1670; lace cravat/jabot ⇒ c. 1660-1790; perfectly regular machine lace ⇒ after 1809.
techniques.lookFor: Openwork fabric built only from thread, with no woven ground: geometric reticella and pointed 'punto in aria' edges early, heavy sculptural Venetian gros point mid-17th c., then filmy floral meshes (Brussels, Mechlin, Valenciennes) in the 18th.
techniques.blurb: Lace has no medieval ancestry; it bursts out of 16th-century cutwork and braid-making, with the first pattern books in the 1520s-1550s. Collar and cuff shapes in portraits date sitters to within a decade or two.

techniques.name: Indian painted & printed cotton (chintz) and its imitations

arrivals.place: Egypt (Indian resist-dyed cottons at Berenike, then Fustat)
arrivals.note: Fustat block-printed fragments mostly 10th-15th c.
craze c. 1660-1720; bans in France 1686, Britain 1700 and 1721

techniques.rule: Flowering-tree palampore or floral chintz made for Europe ⇒ c. 1650-1800 (eras 1500-1750, 1750-2000). European printed cotton ⇒ after c. 1680 and mostly after 1750; single-colour engraved pastoral scenes (toile) ⇒ after 1752-60; small-repeat roller prints ⇒ after 1783.
techniques.lookFor: Hand-drawn or block-printed designs in fast madder reds, purples and indigo blue on white cotton, often glazed; sinuous tree on a rocky mound with exotic flowers. Copperplate toiles are monochrome with fine engraved shading.
techniques.blurb: Indian dyers had mastered mordants that made colours wash-fast centuries before Europe could. The flood of chintz after 1600 provoked import bans, industrial espionage, and ultimately the European cotton-printing industry.

techniques.name: Jacquard loom

arrivals.note: Paisley shawls imitate Kashmir c. 1820-1870

techniques.rule: Large, perfectly repeated pictorial weave (woven portraits, coverlets with eagles and dates, Paisley shawls with huge elongated cones) ⇒ after 1804, i.e. final era. Earlier figured silks were drawloom-woven with shorter, simpler repeats.
techniques.lookFor: Mechanically exact repeats, very large pattern units, woven inscriptions and dates in a corner block, pictorial shading achieved in weave structure.
techniques.blurb: Punched cards replaced the drawboy who lifted warp threads, making complex patterns cheap. Kashmir shawl designs grew from small buta sprigs to full 'paisley' fields largely because Jacquard looms in Europe could imitate them.

techniques.name: Synthetic aniline dyes

arrivals.note: harsh aniline red and purple in late ukiyo-e

techniques.rule: Electric mauve, magenta, acid green or hot orange in any textile, print or beadwork ⇒ after 1856, and outside Europe after c. 1865-1880: final era, and late in it.
techniques.lookFor: Colours that look too bright, cold and uniform for natural dyes, often faded unevenly or bled at the edges; natural palettes are madder red, indigo blue, weld yellow, cochineal crimson, browns.
techniques.blurb: William Perkin's accidental mauve started the chemical dye industry; within twenty years synthetic colours had reached village weavers from Anatolia to Arizona. Dealers treat their presence as a hard dating line.

techniques.name: Featherwork

arrivals.note: Christian images in hummingbird feathers, c. 1530-1700
collected 16th-17th c.
surviving examples collected from 1778
ancient craft; surviving pieces mostly Qing

techniques.rule: Hawaiian red-and-yellow feather cloak or helmet ⇒ c. 1700-1850 (final era or the tail of 1500-1750). Mexican feather mosaic with Christian subject ⇒ 1530-1700. Andean feather tabards survive from c. 200 BCE onward; rectangular blue/yellow panels ⇒ Wari c. 600-900.
techniques.lookFor: Thousands of tiny feathers tied or glued in overlapping rows; Hawaiian: crescents and triangles in red and yellow on netting; Andean: feathers knotted to cotton strings and sewn to cloth in bold blocks.
techniques.blurb: Feathers were worth more than gold to the Aztecs and marked chiefly rank in Hawai'i. The traditions are unrelated, and the survival rate is so poor that find-spot and collection history do most of the dating.

techniques.name: Barkcloth (tapa, kapa, amate)

arrivals.place: Western Polynesia (Tonga, Samoa, Fiji) with Lapita settlers

techniques.rule: Any surviving decorated Pacific barkcloth ⇒ collected after Cook's voyages, so 1768+ (final era, at most the last decades of 1500-1750). Printed text, commemorative lettering or aniline colours on tapa ⇒ after c. 1850.
techniques.lookFor: Felted, papery, non-woven sheet, cream to brown, with rubbed, stencilled or freehand designs in brown and black; visible beater-mark watermarks. Fijian masi: bold black-and-brown stencils; Hawaiian kapa: fine printed geometric lines; Tongan ngatu: huge rubbed panels.
techniques.blurb: Barkcloth beaters go back to Neolithic south China and travelled with the Austronesians across the Pacific. The material is so perishable that the museum record effectively starts in the 1770s.

techniques.name: Cuneiform

arrivals.note: proto-Elamite, then borrowed Mesopotamian cuneiform
Old Assyrian merchant tablets

end.note: last dated tablet is an astronomical text of 75 CE; effectively dead outside temples by the Hellenistic period

techniques.rule: Wedge-impressed clay tablet ⇒ c. 3300 BCE-75 CE, in practice 2600-300 BCE. Pictographic numerical tablets ⇒ before c. 2900 BCE. Small pillow-shaped tablets in envelopes ⇒ Old Assyrian/Old Babylonian (c. 1950-1600 BCE). Large stone reliefs with cuneiform across the figures ⇒ Neo-Assyrian (c. 880-610 BCE).
techniques.lookFor: Clusters of triangular-headed wedges pressed into clay or cut in stone, in ruled lines; early signs are still picture-like and curvilinear, later ones fully abstract.
techniques.blurb: The first writing began as accountancy in Uruk and ended as astronomy in Babylon 3,400 years later. It was used for a dozen unrelated languages from Iran to Egypt.

techniques.name: Egyptian hieroglyphs

end.note: last hieroglyphic inscription at Philae, 394 CE; last demotic graffito 452 CE

techniques.rule: Hieroglyphs ⇒ c. 3250 BCE-394 CE. Cartouche (oval ring round a royal name) ⇒ after c. 2600 BCE. Greek alongside hieroglyphs, or crowded, small, crudely cut signs on temple walls ⇒ Ptolemaic/Roman (after 332 BCE). Coptic letters ⇒ after c. 200 CE.
techniques.lookFor: Small pictures of birds, people, tools and animals in rows or columns, facing the start of the line; royal names in ovals. Hieratic and demotic are cursive ink scripts on papyrus and ostraca.
techniques.blurb: The script appears on bone labels at Abydos around 3250 BCE and stays remarkably stable for 3,600 years. Its end was abrupt: once the temples closed, nobody could read it until 1822.

techniques.name: The alphabet

arrivals.note: first securely dated in Ashoka's edicts; derivation from Aramaic is debated

techniques.rule: Greek or Latin letters ⇒ after c. 775/650 BCE. Any Indic script ⇒ after c. 300 BCE (Indus signs excepted). Runes ⇒ after c. 150 CE; Cyrillic ⇒ after c. 890; Hangul ⇒ after 1446. Lower-case Latin (minuscule) ⇒ after c. 780; Gothic blackletter ⇒ c. 1150-1500; roman/italic type ⇒ after 1465.
techniques.lookFor: Short inventory of 20-30 simple linear signs. Archaic Greek runs right-to-left or boustrophedon with odd letter forms; Latin capitals with serifs = Roman imperial; Brahmi is rounded stick figures and circles.
techniques.blurb: Every alphabet in use descends, by borrowing or inspiration, from one invention by Semitic speakers working with Egyptian signs. Its staged spread gives a ladder of earliest-possible dates for inscribed objects.

techniques.name: Chinese characters

arrivals.note: Han conquest
Han commanderies
inscribed swords of the 5th c.; kana syllabaries develop c. 800-900

arrivals.place: Liao, Xi Xia, Jin (Khitan, Tangut, Jurchen scripts modelled on Chinese)

techniques.rule: Chinese writing ⇒ after c. 1250 BCE. Pictographic oracle-bone or bronze script ⇒ Shang/Zhou; curvy uniform seal script ⇒ standardised 221 BCE (later used for seals); flat clerical script with flared strokes ⇒ Han; standard regular script (kaishu) ⇒ after c. 200-400 CE. Japanese kana mixed in ⇒ after c. 900 CE. Reign marks on porcelain bases ⇒ after c. 1400.
techniques.lookFor: Square logographic characters in columns read top-down, right to left. Kana are simpler, rounded cursive signs between the characters; Hangul is built of circles and straight strokes in blocks.
techniques.blurb: The script is already fully formed on Shang divination bones, with no known local precursors. Script style is a dating tool in itself, and inscriptions on bronzes get longer through the Western Zhou.

techniques.name: Mesoamerican writing, Long Count dates & screenfold books

arrivals.note: Tikal Stela 29; last Long Count monument 909 CE at Tonina
deerskin and bark-paper screenfolds; colonial codices on European paper 1540-1600

end.note: glyphic literacy suppressed after the conquest; last Maya scribes at Tayasal fall in 1697

techniques.rule: Maya stela or panel with Long Count date ⇒ 292-909 CE (eras 250-500 to 750-1000). Square glyph blocks on carved stone or pots ⇒ Classic Maya. Aztec/Mixtec screenfold pictorials ⇒ c. 1200-1600; alphabetic glosses in Spanish or Nahuatl ⇒ after 1521. No writing on Andean objects before 1532.
techniques.lookFor: Maya glyphs: rounded 'pebble' blocks in paired columns with bar-and-dot numbers (bar = 5, dot = 1). Mixtec/Aztec: cartoon-like figures, footprints for travel, day signs with dots, no long texts.
techniques.blurb: Mesoamerica is the one place in the Americas with true writing, and Maya monuments are dated to the day. The carved-date habit starts and stops abruptly, bracketing the Classic period.

techniques.name: Papyrus

arrivals.place: Merovingian Gaul & papal chancery (last western use)
arrivals.note: papal bulls on papyrus until the 11th c.

end.note: replaced by parchment in Europe (4th-8th c.) and by paper in Egypt (10th c.)

techniques.rule: Papyrus sheet or roll ⇒ Egypt/Mediterranean, c. 2900 BCE-1000 CE. Book of the Dead with coloured vignettes ⇒ New Kingdom to Ptolemaic (c. 1550-30 BCE). Greek on papyrus ⇒ after 332 BCE in Egypt; Coptic ⇒ after c. 250 CE; Arabic ⇒ after 641.
techniques.lookFor: Tan sheet with a visible criss-cross of plant fibres (horizontal on one face, vertical on the other), brittle ragged edges, written in black and red ink with a reed.
techniques.blurb: Papyrus was Egypt's export monopoly for almost four thousand years. Nearly all surviving examples come from Egypt's dry sand, so the place guess is easy and the script tells the era.

techniques.name: Parchment codex & illuminated manuscripts

arrivals.note: purple-dyed and gold-ground luxury books
Durrow, Lindisfarne, Kells, c. 680-800
private prayer books, peak 1350-1520

end.note: printing ends routine manuscript production in Europe; illumination lingers for luxury books

techniques.rule: Bound book (not a roll) ⇒ after c. 100 CE, standard after c. 350. Illuminated parchment leaf ⇒ c. 400-1520. Interlace carpet pages ⇒ Insular c. 650-850; gold-leaf backgrounds and tiny Gothic script ⇒ 1200-1400; realistic flower-strewn borders with cast shadows ⇒ Flemish 1470-1530. Horizontal-format Kufic Qur'an leaf ⇒ c. 750-1000.
techniques.lookFor: Smooth, slightly translucent animal skin with hair-side/flesh-side colour difference, ruled lines, pricking; burnished gold leaf, blue and red penwork initials. Paper manuscripts show laid lines and are common only after c. 1350 in Europe.
techniques.blurb: The codex was a Roman notebook format that early Christians adopted wholesale; by 400 it had displaced the scroll. A thousand years of book painting followed, each century with unmistakable script and border fashions.

techniques.name: Paper

arrivals.note: traditionally after the battle of Talas
replaces palm leaf from the 13th-15th c.
watermarks from 1282

techniques.rule: Work on paper ⇒ China after c. 100 BCE (as a writing surface after c. 100 CE); Islamic lands after c. 750-800; India after c. 1200 (mostly 1350+); Europe after c. 1100 in Spain, 1270 in Italy, c. 1400 north of the Alps. Watermark ⇒ European, after 1282. Wove paper (no laid lines) ⇒ after 1757. Wood-pulp paper that has gone brown and brittle ⇒ after c. 1850.
techniques.lookFor: Felted fibre sheet; held to light, pre-1800 European paper shows parallel 'laid' lines and widely spaced chain lines plus a watermark. Islamic paper is burnished glossy; East Asian paper is thin, long-fibred, often mounted on silk.
techniques.blurb: Cai Lun's report to the throne in 105 CE is the traditional birthday, though excavated scraps are two centuries older. Paper took a thousand years to cross from Luoyang to Spain, mostly along the same road as Islam.

techniques.name: Palm-leaf manuscripts

arrivals.note: Kushan-era Sanskrit leaves preserved in Xinjiang
oldest dated complete manuscripts, 9th c.
on palm leaf to c. 1350, then paper

end.note: replaced by paper in north India c. 1350-1450; continues in south India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia into the 20th c.

techniques.rule: Illustrated palm-leaf folio from eastern India/Nepal ⇒ c. 1000-1250 (era 1000-1250). North Indian manuscript on paper keeping the long narrow format ⇒ after c. 1350. Most surviving South Indian, Sri Lankan, Balinese and Burmese palm-leaf books ⇒ 1700-1950, because leaves last only a few centuries in the tropics.
techniques.lookFor: Long narrow strips (about 5 x 30-60 cm) with one or two string holes, text incised and inked or written with reed pen, stacked between wooden covers. Miniatures are small squares between text blocks.
techniques.blurb: The palm leaf dictated the shape of South and Southeast Asian books, and even of the rounded letters of southern scripts (straight lines would split the leaf). Paper's arrival in the 14th century let Indian painters go taller and bigger.

techniques.name: Woodblock printing

arrivals.note: Mugujeonggwang dharani, c. 704-751
Hyakumanto dharani, 764-770
block-printed Arabic amulets, c. 900-1400

arrivals.place: Germany, France & Italy (woodcut prints, playing cards)

techniques.rule: Printed text or image on paper ⇒ East Asia after c. 660-700; Europe after c. 1400. European woodcut with fine cross-hatching ⇒ after Durer, c. 1495; chiaroscuro woodcut ⇒ after 1508. Japanese single-sheet prints ⇒ after c. 1670.
techniques.lookFor: Bold black relief lines with slight ink squash at the edges, no plate mark; wood-grain breaks and worm-holes in late impressions. East Asian books: thin paper printed one side and folded.
techniques.blurb: Printing from carved blocks is a Buddhist merit-making technology of the 7th-8th century; the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book. Europe reinvented or imported the idea around 1400, just ahead of Gutenberg.

techniques.name: Movable type & the printing press

arrivals.note: Jikji, 1377, is the oldest surviving metal-type book
press, oil ink and cast alloy type

techniques.rule: Typeset printed page in Europe ⇒ after 1450 (first era possible: 1250-1500, and only its last 50 years). Printed in the Americas ⇒ after 1539; in Arabic script by Muslims ⇒ after 1727, commonly after c. 1820. Title page, page numbers, roman type ⇒ after c. 1470-1500.
techniques.lookFor: Perfectly regular repeated letterforms with slight impression into the paper; incunables imitate manuscripts with hand-coloured initials. Blackletter type = German lands or before c. 1530 elsewhere; roman and italic = Italian-style humanist printing.
techniques.blurb: East Asia had movable type four centuries before Gutenberg, but thousands of characters made woodblocks more practical there. In Europe, 26 letters plus a wine-press produced some twenty million books by 1500.

techniques.name: Engraving, etching, mezzotint, aquatint

arrivals.note: Daniel Hopfer; first dated etching 1513
'the English manner'

techniques.rule: Engraving ⇒ after c. 1435; etching ⇒ after c. 1500; mezzotint ⇒ after 1642; aquatint ⇒ after 1768; steel engraving ⇒ after c. 1820. So any intaglio print is era 1250-1500 at the earliest, and velvety tonal prints are 1650+.
techniques.lookFor: A rectangular plate-mark dent around the image. Engraving: crisp swelling-and-tapering lines; etching: freer, even-width wiry lines; mezzotint: soft continuous tones emerging from black; aquatint: flat grainy washes like watercolour.
techniques.blurb: Goldsmiths who engraved metal for niello began inking their plates and printing them around 1430. Each later invention added tone, and each has a well-documented birth date.

techniques.name: Lithography & chromolithography

arrivals.note: Currier & Ives from 1835
Kalighat-style and Ravi Varma oleographs later
lithographed books keep the look of calligraphy

techniques.rule: Lithograph ⇒ after 1796, in practice after c. 1815; colour-printed labels, posters, trade cards ⇒ after 1837 and mostly after 1870: all final era. Printed Persian, Urdu or Arabic books in flowing calligraphic hand ⇒ lithographed, after c. 1830.
techniques.lookFor: No plate mark and no relief; a greasy crayon or wash texture with a fine random grain; colour areas built from overlapping flat tints or stipple dots.
techniques.blurb: Drawing on limestone with grease let artists print without engraving skills. It suited cursive scripts so well that the Islamic world and India adopted lithography decades before type.

techniques.name: Photographic processes

arrivals.note: daguerreotype dominant to c. 1855
hand-coloured albumen tourist prints 1865-1900

techniques.rule: Any photograph ⇒ after 1839 (final era). Daguerreotype (mirror image in a case) ⇒ 1839-1860; ambrotype/tintype ⇒ 1854-1900; albumen print, carte-de-visite ⇒ 1855-1895; cabinet card ⇒ 1866-1910; gelatin silver ⇒ 1885 onward; colour ⇒ autochrome 1907, Kodachrome 1935.
techniques.lookFor: Daguerreotype: silvery mirror plate that flips positive/negative with angle. Albumen: thin glossy paper on card, warm purple-brown, yellowed highlights. Gelatin silver: neutral black-grey, sometimes silvering-out in shadows.
techniques.blurb: Photography spread worldwide in about five years, faster than any earlier image technology. Process, mount and card format date a photograph to within a decade.

techniques.name: Egyptian blue (and Han blue/purple)

arrivals.note: barium copper silicates, separate invention; late Western Zhou beads, common Warring States-Han, gone after c. 220 CE

arrivals.place: Roman provinces (wall painting from Britain to Syria)

end.note: manufacture lapses after the Roman period; only sporadic medieval use

techniques.rule: A clear mid-blue pigment on an object from the ancient Mediterranean or Near East ⇒ Egyptian blue, so c. 3250 BCE-500 CE. Blue on medieval and later works is azurite, ultramarine, smalt or indigo. Blue/purple on Qin-Han terracotta or pots ⇒ c. 800 BCE-220 CE, mostly 475 BCE-220 CE.
techniques.lookFor: A slightly greenish, granular sky-to-turquoise blue, often coarse and sparkling, on Egyptian coffins, wall paintings, Greek sculpture traces and Roman frescoes; ultramarine is deeper and more violet.
techniques.blurb: The first synthetic pigment, a calcium copper silicate cooked from sand, lime and copper. China independently made barium analogues that colour the Terracotta Army. Both recipes were then forgotten.

techniques.name: Lapis lazuli & ultramarine

arrivals.place: Central Asian cave murals (Kizil, Bamiyan) as pigment
arrivals.note: first substantial use ground as ultramarine paint
costlier than gold; reserved for the Virgin's robe

techniques.rule: Lapis inlay or beads in Egypt/Mesopotamia ⇒ any time after c. 3500 BCE (strong in Early Dynastic Ur, Middle and New Kingdom Egypt). Deep violet-blue paint in European painting ⇒ after c. 1000 and common 1280-1700. Cheap, saturated ultramarine across large areas ⇒ after 1828.
techniques.lookFor: Stone: intense royal blue with gold pyrite flecks and white calcite veins. Pigment: deep, warm, slightly violet blue, unlike greenish azurite or Egyptian blue.
techniques.blurb: For over five thousand years nearly all lapis came from one valley in Afghanistan, so its presence maps ancient trade. As paint it only became common in the Middle Ages, and a chemist's synthetic version ended its mystique in 1828.

techniques.name: Encaustic mummy portraits (Fayum)

arrivals.note: the technique's Christian afterlife, 6th-7th c.

end.note: panel portraits on mummies cease in the mid-3rd century

techniques.rule: Naturalistic bust portrait on a thin wooden panel or linen shroud from Egypt ⇒ c. 30-260 CE (era 0-250). Hairstyles follow imperial fashion: Flavian curls (c. 70-100), Trajanic buns, bearded men after Hadrian (117+).
techniques.lookFor: Life-size frontal face with large dark eyes, highlights and shadow, Roman dress and jewellery, wax paint with visible tool strokes (or matte tempera); panel edges cut to fit mummy wrappings.
techniques.blurb: These are the only large body of painted portraits to survive from the classical world: Roman-style likenesses on Egyptian mummies. The wax medium kept colours startlingly fresh.

techniques.name: Fresco & plaster wall painting

arrivals.note: Four Styles, c. 150 BCE-79 CE
tempera on dry plaster; main phase c. 460-480 CE
true fresco, c. 200-600 CE; Maya Bonampak 791

techniques.rule: Detached wall-painting fragment: Aegean marine/bull-leaping style ⇒ c. 1700-1200 BCE; Roman red/black panels with architecture or garden views ⇒ c. 100 BCE-100 CE; Central Asian/Chinese Buddhist murals ⇒ c. 400-1000 CE; Italian narrative fresco ⇒ 1280-1600.
techniques.lookFor: Matte, chalky surface on plaster with visible plaster-patch joins (giornate), incised guide lines, and losses that expose white lime. Teotihuacan: flat red-dominated palette with repeating priests and felines.
techniques.blurb: Painting into wet lime plaster binds pigment into the wall. Minoans did it in the Bronze Age, Rome made it routine, and Teotihuacan arrived at it separately on the other side of the world.

techniques.name: Gold-ground tempera panels & icons

arrivals.note: Russian schools: Novgorod 12th-15th c., Rublev c. 1410, Stroganov c. 1600

arrivals.place: Tuscany (maniera greca, then Duccio and Giotto)

arrivals.note: exports to Venice; to c. 1700
panel icons and triptychs from the 15th c.; yellow replaces gold

techniques.rule: Italian altarpiece panel with tooled gold background ⇒ c. 1230-1450 (era 1000-1250 end, mostly 1250-1500); landscape or sky replaces gold after c. 1450. Orthodox icons keep gold grounds to the present, so use style: metal oklad covers and westernised faces ⇒ 1650+. Ethiopian panel icons ⇒ after c. 1450.
techniques.lookFor: Egg tempera in fine hatched strokes on gessoed wood, burnished gold leaf with punched haloes, red bole showing through wear; frontal saints with Greek or Slavonic name inscriptions.
techniques.blurb: The devotional gold-ground panel was Byzantium's export to both Russia and Italy. In the West it lasted barely two centuries before perspective and oil paint replaced heaven's gold with landscape.

techniques.name: Oil painting (and oil on canvas)

arrivals.note: isolated early use of drying oils
Cusco School flourishes c. 1650-1800
suppressed 1614; yoga oil painting resumes in the 1870s
Ravi Varma from the 1870s

techniques.rule: Oil painting with blended, glazed modelling ⇒ after c. 1420 in the Netherlands, c. 1475 in Italy. Oil on canvas ⇒ after c. 1500 (panel still common in the north to c. 1650). Oil painting made in the Americas ⇒ after c. 1550; in East or South Asia ⇒ after c. 1700 except rare Jesuit works.
techniques.lookFor: Deep translucent shadows, soft transitions, glossy varnish, canvas weave or craquelure visible; impasto highlights. Tempera looks drier, lighter and hatched.
techniques.blurb: Drying oils were known earlier, but Jan van Eyck's generation made oil the vehicle for illusionistic painting. Venice paired it with canvas, and that combination then travelled with European empires.

techniques.name: Linear (one-point) perspective

arrivals.note: Durer's treatise 1525
via Jesuit gifts of Flemish engravings
Okumura Masanobu; later Hokusai and Hiroshige

techniques.rule: Consistent vanishing-point perspective ⇒ after c. 1420 in Italy, c. 1460 in northern Europe, c. 1580 in India, c. 1715 in China, c. 1740 in Japan. Tiled floors and buildings receding to a single point never occur in medieval, Byzantine, pre-1700 East Asian or pre-contact American art.
techniques.lookFor: Check floor tiles, ceilings and street facades: do the orthogonals meet at one point on the horizon? Pre-perspective images tilt the ground up, stack distant figures higher, or use parallel (axonometric) lines as in Chinese and Japanese scrolls.
techniques.blurb: Brunelleschi demonstrated it, Masaccio painted it (1427) and Alberti wrote the rules (1435). Its arrival in Asian painting can be traced to specific Jesuit missions and Dutch prints.

techniques.name: Handscrolls, hanging scrolls & ink landscape

arrivals.note: Five Dynasties-Northern Song
cloth scroll paintings; oldest survivors 11th c.
yamato-e; Tale of Genji scrolls

arrivals.place: China (literati ink painting with long inscriptions and seals)
arrivals.note: Yuan masters onward
Momoyama and Edo

techniques.rule: Vertical ink landscape scroll ⇒ after c. 950. Painting with the artist's poem, signature and many red collector seals in the image ⇒ after c. 1300. Japanese gold-leaf screens ⇒ after c. 1570. Tibetan thangka ⇒ after c. 1050, mostly 1400-1950. Surviving paintings on silk before 900 are very rare.
techniques.lookFor: Silk or paper mounted on brocade with a roller; monochrome ink washes with empty space as mist; red seals. Thangkas: symmetrical deity in mineral reds and blues inside brocade borders.
techniques.blurb: The scroll formats fix a rough sequence: narrative handscrolls first, towering Song landscapes on hanging scrolls next, then the scholar-amateur's ink play covered in inscriptions. Japan and Korea adopted each stage a century or two later.

techniques.name: Ukiyo-e & full-colour woodblock printing

end.note: displaced by lithography and photography; shin-hanga revival from 1915
