techniques.rule: Japanese woodblock print in many colours ⇒ after 1765 (so final era). Black-only or hand-coloured ⇒ c. 1670-1765 (era 1500-1750). Strong synthetic blue skies and water ⇒ after 1829-31. Garish aniline red and purple, Western dress, trains ⇒ Meiji, after 1868.
techniques.lookFor: Flat colour areas with black keyblock outlines, no shading, cropped asymmetrical compositions, publisher and censor seals, signature cartouches; standard oban sheet c. 25 x 38 cm.
techniques.blurb: Ukiyo-e began as cheap black-line pictures of the pleasure quarters. Harunobu's calendar prints of 1765 introduced multi-block registration, and imported Prussian blue around 1830 launched the landscape craze.

techniques.name: Prussian blue
techniques.rule: Dark, slightly greenish synthetic blue ⇒ after 1706; in Japanese prints after c. 1829. It is a firm 'not before 1700' marker; other 19th-century synthetics (cobalt blue 1802, chrome yellow c. 1815, emerald green 1814, synthetic ultramarine 1828, cadmium yellow c. 1840s) push later still.
techniques.lookFor: Intense inky blue that grades smoothly from near-black to pale sky in washes (bokashi in Japanese prints); earlier Japanese prints use fugitive dayflower blue or dull indigo, now faded to grey-buff.
techniques.blurb: The first modern synthetic pigment was a Berlin colour-maker's accident. Cheap and strong, it spread worldwide within decades and is routinely used by conservators to expose 'old master' fakes.

techniques.name: Persian miniature painting

arrivals.note: Maqamat and scientific manuscripts, c. 1200-1258

arrivals.place: Delhi & Agra (Mughal atelier founded by Persian masters)

end.note: Qajar painting turns to oil, lacquer and photography-influenced realism

techniques.rule: Persian book painting with Chinese-style clouds, dragons and gnarled trees ⇒ after the Mongol conquest, c. 1300. High horizon, jewel colours, tiled architecture ⇒ Timurid/Safavid 1400-1600. Tall baton turbans (taj) ⇒ Safavid 1501-1550. Single languid youths with calligraphic line ⇒ Isfahan c. 1590-1700. European shading ⇒ after c. 1670.
techniques.lookFor: Small opaque-watercolour paintings set within text panels of nasta'liq script; flat pure colour, gold skies, figures shown without shadows, ground tilted up like a carpet.
techniques.blurb: Illustrated Persian books take off under the Mongol Ilkhans, who brought Chinese pictorial ideas west. Each dynasty's style is distinct, and exiled Safavid painters founded both the Ottoman and Mughal schools.

techniques.name: Mughal, Deccani, Rajput & Pahari miniature painting

arrivals.place: Western India (Jain and Sultanate manuscripts, precursor)
arrivals.note: paper manuscripts with protruding 'further eye', c. 1350-1550
lyrical Krishna subjects, c. 1770-1830
natural-history and trades for British patrons

end.note: court ateliers decline with British rule and photography

techniques.rule: Indian miniature with naturalistic portraits, shading and recession ⇒ Mughal, after c. 1580. Profile ruler with halo on a terrace ⇒ c. 1615-1800. Hot flat red/yellow grounds with bold figures ⇒ Rajput (1600-1800) or Basohli (1670-1730). Soft, pale, lyrical landscapes with Radha and Krishna ⇒ Kangra, 1770-1830 (final era). Watercolour studies of birds/trades on English paper ⇒ Company, 1775-1860.
techniques.lookFor: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper with decorated album borders; Mughal: fine stippled modelling, individual likenesses; Rajput: bright colour blocks, large almond eyes, Devanagari captions.
techniques.blurb: Akbar's workshop fused Persian technique, Indian colour and European engravings from 1560. As Mughal patronage shrank, painters carried the style to Rajput and hill courts, where it became more devotional and less naturalistic.

techniques.name: Greek sculpture: kouros to contrapposto

arrivals.note: emotional, twisting, realistic; 323-31 BCE

techniques.rule: Stiff frontal nude youth, left foot forward, fists clenched, 'archaic smile' ⇒ c. 620-480 BCE (era 750-500 BCE). Relaxed weight-shift pose with tilted hips ⇒ after c. 480 BCE. Extreme twisting, pathos, old age, children ⇒ Hellenistic, after c. 323 BCE. In late antiquity (after c. 300 CE) figures turn frontal and blocky again.
techniques.lookFor: Kouros: symmetrical, patterned hair in beads, almond eyes, anatomy as surface grooves. Classical: one engaged and one free leg, S-curve through the torso, calm idealised face.
techniques.blurb: Greek sculptors took the Egyptian striding pose and in about 140 years turned it into the naturalistic standing figure. Contrapposto then became the default of Roman, Gandharan and Renaissance sculpture.

techniques.name: Roman marble portraiture

arrivals.place: Roman provinces (Gaul, Spain, North Africa, Asia Minor)
Egypt (painted mummy portraits and plaster masks)

end.note: individualised portrait sculpture dies out in the 5th century

techniques.rule: Warts-and-all elderly face ⇒ late Republic, c. 100-30 BCE. Smooth ageless classicism ⇒ Augustan/Julio-Claudian (27 BCE-68 CE). Women's towering curled hair ⇒ Flavian (70-100). Bearded emperor/man and drilled or incised pupils and irises ⇒ after Hadrian, c. 120-130 CE. Cropped stubble hair, anxious brow ⇒ 3rd century. Huge staring eyes, rigid frontality ⇒ after c. 300.
techniques.lookFor: White marble head or bust; look at the eyes (blank eyeballs were painted and are earlier; carved pupils are later), the beard, deep drill channels in hair, and the bust shape (small chest patch early, full torso with arms later).
techniques.blurb: Roman portrait fashions followed the reigning emperor and empress closely, so hair and beard date a head to a generation. The carved pupil and the Hadrianic beard arrive together around 120-130 CE.

techniques.name: Olmec colossal heads & carved jade

arrivals.place: Central Mexico & Guerrero (Olmec-style ceramics, jades, cave paintings)

end.note: La Venta abandoned; Epi-Olmec and Izapan styles follow

techniques.rule: Basalt colossal head, 'baby-face' hollow white ceramic figure, or jade were-jaguar with downturned mouth and cleft head ⇒ Olmec, c. 1200-400 BCE (eras 1250-1000 through 500-250 BCE). It predates everything Maya Classic, Teotihuacan or Aztec by at least 600 years.
techniques.lookFor: Fleshy faces with thick everted lips, flat nose, snarling downturned mouth, helmet-like headgear; blue-green jade celts and masks polished to a high gloss with fine incised lines.
techniques.blurb: The Olmec of the Gulf Coast set Mesoamerica's artistic agenda: monumental stone portraiture, jade as the supreme material, and the feline-human supernatural. Their heads weigh up to 40 tons and the stone was moved 60 km or more.

techniques.name: West African terracotta sculpture (Nok, Ife, Djenne)

arrivals.note: naturalistic terracotta heads alongside brass, c. 1100-1450
kneeling and snake-covered figures, c. 1100-1500

techniques.rule: Nok head (triangular pierced eyes, elaborate coiffure) ⇒ c. 900 BCE-1 CE (eras 1000-750 BCE through 250-0 BCE; guess c. 500-200 BCE). Mali terracotta figures ⇒ c. 1100-1500. Ife terracotta ⇒ c. 1100-1450. These are the main sub-Saharan sculptures datable before 1500.
techniques.lookFor: Nok: hollow, coarse gritty orange clay, D-shaped or triangular eyes with drilled pupils, arched brows, detailed jewellery. Djenne: reddish slip, bulging eyes, figures kneeling or hugging knees, bodies with snakes or pustules.
techniques.blurb: Nok is the oldest large-scale figurative sculpture in sub-Saharan Africa and appears alongside early iron-working. Its end, around the turn of the era, leaves a gap of a thousand years before Ife and Djenne.

techniques.name: Survival horizon for wood sculpture (Africa, Oceania, Northwest Coast)

arrivals.note: rare dry-cave survivals from the 11th-15th c.

arrivals.place: Polynesia & Melanesia (first collected on Cook's voyages)
Northwest Coast of North America (first collected)

techniques.rule: Wooden mask or figure from sub-Saharan Africa, the Pacific or the Northwest Coast ⇒ assume 1750-2000, and usually 1850-1950. Wood rarely lasts two centuries in the tropics, and European collecting began c. 1770 (Pacific, Northwest Coast) and c. 1870-1900 (inland Africa). Exceptions: Dogon/Tellem cave figures, waterlogged or arid-site finds.
techniques.lookFor: Carved wood with patina from handling, kaolin and ochre pigment, raffia, shell, trade-cloth or glass-bead attachments, nails and mirrors (Kongo nkisi). European trade materials confirm a post-contact date.
techniques.blurb: The traditions are older than the objects. For the game the practical rule is statistical: almost every museum's African, Oceanic and Northwest Coast wood sculpture was made within a lifetime of being collected.

techniques.name: Hindu temple images (multi-armed deities)

arrivals.note: Khmer style to 1431
processional bronzes c. 950-1250, continuing under Vijayanagara

techniques.rule: Stone or bronze image of Vishnu, Shiva, Durga or Ganesha with multiple arms ⇒ after c. 100 BCE in India (standard forms from c. 100-400 CE), c. 500 in Southeast Asia. Nataraja in a ring of flames ⇒ after c. 950 (era 750-1000 end onward). Khmer Hindu images ⇒ c. 550-1300; Javanese ⇒ c. 700-1500.
techniques.lookFor: Frontal deity with attributes held in four or more hands (discus, conch, trident, mace), tall crown or matted locks, on a lotus or animal vehicle. Chola bronzes: slender, sway-hipped, with lugs for carrying poles.
techniques.blurb: Hindu gods acquired their standard sculpted forms under the Kushans and Guptas, at the same time and in the same workshops as the Buddha image. Indian traders and Brahmins carried them to Southeast Asia within a few centuries.

techniques.name: Lacquer (urushi)

arrivals.note: equally early or earlier finds; independence debated
Warring States and Han tomb lacquers, c. 450 BCE-220 CE
Southern Song-Yuan; imperial workshops in the Ming
varnished painting, a different material
shellac and varnish, not true lacquer

techniques.rule: Red-and-black painted lacquer cups, boxes and coffins with swirling clouds ⇒ China c. 450 BCE-220 CE. Deeply carved red lacquer ⇒ after c. 1250, mostly Ming-Qing (1400-1900). Black lacquer with gold chinoiserie on European furniture ⇒ after c. 1680. Persian/Kashmiri painted pen boxes and bookbindings ⇒ after c. 1500, mostly 1700-1900.
techniques.lookFor: Deep glossy black or vermilion surface, light wooden or cloth core, fine crackle. Carved lacquer shows layer-lines in the cut walls; japanning is flatter, less deep, often crazed and yellowed.
techniques.blurb: Lacquer is the sap of an East Asian tree, so true lacquerware is made only where the tree grows (or imported). Europe's longing for it produced a whole imitation industry from the 1680s.

techniques.name: Maki-e (sprinkled-gold lacquer) & export lacquer

arrivals.place: Nagasaki (Nanban export lacquer for Portugal and Spain)
arrivals.note: domed coffers with shell inlay, c. 1580-1639

arrivals.place: Netherlands & France (pictorial-style imports cut into furniture)
Japan (inro and small Edo luxury wares)
arrivals.note: inro with netsuke, c. 1650-1870

techniques.rule: Gold-powder designs on black lacquer ⇒ Japan after c. 800; most surviving pieces Edo/Meiji (1600-1912). Chests densely covered in gold foliage and mother-of-pearl ⇒ Nanban export c. 1580-1639. Inro (tiered belt case) ⇒ c. 1600-1880.
techniques.lookFor: Gold or silver powder sprinkled into wet lacquer giving a soft granular metallic picture, flat (hiramaki-e), polished flush (togidashi) or raised (takamaki-e); sparse asymmetrical nature motifs, nashiji 'pear-skin' gold fleck grounds.
techniques.blurb: Maki-e is Japan's signature lacquer technique, perfected in the Heian court. The Portuguese and then the Dutch exported it in bulk, and Marie-Antoinette collected it.

techniques.name: Mother-of-pearl inlaid lacquer & wood

arrivals.note: Standard of Ur
introduced under Unified Silla; surviving Goryeo sutra boxes 11th-14th c., then Joseon boxes and chests
exported to Europe and the Ottomans
Qur'an stands, thrones, later Syrian furniture

techniques.rule: East Asian black lacquer with shell-inlaid flowers or figures ⇒ after c. 700; Korean boxes with tiny chrysanthemum scrolls and wire ⇒ Goryeo 1100-1392, bolder designs ⇒ Joseon 1400-1900. Gujarati all-shell caskets ⇒ c. 1520-1650. Shell-inlaid oil paintings ⇒ Mexico 1680-1750.
techniques.lookFor: Iridescent pink-green shell pieces set flush in black or red lacquer or dark wood; Korean work combines shell with twisted brass wire and tortoiseshell; Ottoman work with tortoiseshell and ivory in geometric stars.
techniques.blurb: Shell inlay in lacquer was a Tang court fashion preserved in Japan's Shosoin repository of 756. Korea made it a national speciality, and the Manila galleon carried the taste to Mexico.

techniques.name: Jade carving

arrivals.note: Itoigawa jadeite; magatama peak in Kofun 300-600 CE
to c. 700 CE, then gold
plaques, masks, ear flares to c. 900
hei-tiki and mere; most collected 1770-1900
bright emerald-green jadeite becomes common only in late Qing

techniques.rule: Chinese jade bi discs and cong tubes ⇒ Neolithic (c. 3300-2000 BCE) or later archaising copies. Mesoamerican jade ⇒ c. 1000 BCE-1521 CE, at its height before 900. Vivid emerald-green or lavender jadeite from China ⇒ after c. 1780. Maori pounamu ⇒ after c. 1300, usually 1750-1900. Mughal jade ⇒ after c. 1600.
techniques.lookFor: Chinese nephrite: soft waxy lustre, white, celadon, yellow, brown 'skin'. Jadeite: glassier, brighter greens. Olmec: blue-green; Maya: apple green. Pounamu: dark spinach green, translucent at edges. All are abraded, never chiselled, so edges are soft.
techniques.blurb: Three unrelated cultures (China, Mesoamerica, Maori) made tough green stone their most precious material. In China the stone itself changes: Khotan nephrite for most of history, Burmese jadeite only from the late 18th century.

techniques.name: Afro-Portuguese, Indo-Portuguese & Hispano-Philippine ivories

arrivals.place: Sri Lanka (caskets for the Portuguese court)

arrivals.note: spiral-carved tusks with trade scenes in the 19th c.

arrivals.place: Manila (Chinese carvers; saints for Mexico and Spain)
Canton (export ivory: fans, puzzle balls, models)

techniques.rule: African ivory saltcellar, spoon or hunting horn with European motifs (armillary spheres, Portuguese arms, bearded soldiers) ⇒ c. 1490-1600 (era 1250-1500 tail or 1500-1750). Christian ivory figures with Asian faces ⇒ after 1540, mostly 1600-1800. Pierced concentric balls and brise fans ⇒ Canton 1750-1900.
techniques.lookFor: Elephant ivory with fine cross-hatched 'engine-turned' grain; lidded spherical cups on conical bases with tiny figures (Sapi), high-relief Portuguese with long noses (Benin); Christ Child with slanted eyes and gilt hair (Manila/Goa).
techniques.blurb: Among the first objects made in Africa and Asia specifically for European buyers. Their start dates are fixed by Portuguese arrivals: Sierra Leone in the 1460s, Benin 1485, India 1498, Manila 1571.

techniques.name: Baltic amber trade

arrivals.note: figured pendants, c. 700-400 BCE

techniques.rule: Carved figured amber pendants ⇒ pre-Roman Italy c. 700-400 BCE or Roman Aquileia c. 50-200 CE. Amber spacer-plate necklaces ⇒ Bronze Age Europe/Mycenae c. 1900-1400 BCE. Amber caskets and tankards with ivory ⇒ Baltic 1550-1750.
techniques.lookFor: Translucent honey to cherry-red resin, crazed and darkened to opaque brown crust when ancient; very light. Etruscan pieces are small reclining figures or heads pierced for stringing.
techniques.blurb: Amber is washed up on the south Baltic shore and was carried overland to the Mediterranean from the Bronze Age. Chemical tests show Mycenaean and even Syrian royal amber is Baltic.

techniques.name: Turquoise mosaic (Southwest & Mesoamerica)

arrivals.place: West & Central Mexico (Toltec Tula, Alta Vista)
Mixteca & Aztec empire (masks, shields, double-headed serpent)

arrivals.note: silverwork learned c. 1850-70

end.note: Aztec court production ends with the conquest

techniques.rule: Turquoise mosaic mask, shield or knife handle ⇒ Postclassic Mesoamerica, c. 950-1521 and mostly 1400-1521 (era 1250-1500 / 1500-1750 start). Classic Maya and Teotihuacan used jade and greenstone, not turquoise. Silver jewellery set with turquoise from the Southwest ⇒ after c. 1870.
techniques.lookFor: Hundreds of tiny blue-green tesserae glued with resin onto wood, with shell (red Spondylus, white conch), pyrite and gold; faces of gods, serpents. Navajo/Zuni: chunky stones in stamped silver bezels, squash-blossom necklaces.
techniques.blurb: Turquoise entered Mesoamerica late, after 900, and its sources in the US Southwest and northern Mexico are still being traced. For the Aztecs it was the colour of fire and of rulership.

techniques.name: Anthropomorphic Buddha image

arrivals.note: late Han tomb motifs; earliest dated gilt bronze 338 CE
second conversion; Zanabazar bronzes from the 1680s

techniques.rule: Any Buddha figure ⇒ after c. 50-100 CE; earlier Buddhist art (Sanchi, Bharhut) shows only footprints, an empty throne, wheel or tree. In China ⇒ after c. 200, realistically 400+; Korea ⇒ after 372; Japan ⇒ after 552; Southeast Asia ⇒ after c. 500; Tibet ⇒ after c. 640.
techniques.lookFor: Monk's robe, cranial bump (ushnisha), elongated earlobes, tuft between the brows, hand gestures. Gandhara: grey schist, wavy hair, toga-like folds, Apollo face. Mathura: red spotted sandstone, shaven-head look, clinging robe. Gupta (400s): downcast eyes, wet drapery, huge decorated halo.
techniques.blurb: For about four centuries the Buddha was not shown in human form. The image emerged under the Kushans, perhaps at once in Greek-influenced Gandhara and in Mathura, and then travelled the Silk Road and sea lanes with fixed dates of arrival.

techniques.name: Christian imagery

arrivals.note: cross on Ezana's coins
Faras cathedral murals
Jelling stone
brass crucifixes from the 16th c.

techniques.rule: Christian subject ⇒ after c. 230; chi-rho and imperial Christian art ⇒ after 313; the Crucifixion depicted ⇒ after c. 420, and a dead, slumped Christ on the cross ⇒ after c. 950-1000. By place: Scandinavia/Russia ⇒ after c. 965-988; Americas ⇒ after 1492; Kongo ⇒ after 1491; Japan ⇒ 1549-1639 or after 1860.
techniques.lookFor: Cross, chi-rho, fish, Good Shepherd, haloed apostles, Virgin and Child. Early art avoids the Crucifixion; Romanesque shows Christ alive and crowned, Gothic and later show suffering.
techniques.blurb: Christian art starts cautiously in the 3rd century and becomes public after Constantine. Outside the Roman world, each conversion date is a floor for cross-bearing objects.

techniques.name: Halo / nimbus

arrivals.note: sun-ray crowns on Helios and kings rather than a disc
saints routinely haloed by the 5th-6th c.
with Buddhist imagery
round haloes as generic emphasis; flame haloes for prophets after c. 1300
from Jahangir onward

techniques.rule: Disc halo behind a head ⇒ after c. 100 CE in Buddhist Asia, after c. 320 in Christian art. Square halo ⇒ living donor, Rome c. 600-1100. Flaming gold halo ⇒ Persian/Ottoman after c. 1300. Ruler in profile with a gold sun-halo ⇒ Mughal or Rajput India, after c. 1615. Foreshortened ring halo ⇒ Italy after c. 1430.
techniques.lookFor: A plain or decorated disc, ring, rays or flames behind the head; a cross inside the disc marks Christ; a full-body almond (mandorla) marks glory.
techniques.blurb: The halo is a shared Eurasian invention of the first centuries CE with roots in solar and royal imagery, and whether it began in the Iranian world, the Hellenistic East or Gandhara is unsettled. It reached Christianity through imperial portraiture.

techniques.name: Arabic-script calligraphy & Islamic aniconic ornament

arrivals.note: the hanging script of Persian, Mughal and Ottoman poetry

techniques.rule: Arabic script as decoration ⇒ after c. 690. Angular Kufic ⇒ c. 700-1200 (foliated/knotted Kufic 950-1250); cursive naskh and thuluth on objects ⇒ after c. 1000-1150; sloping nasta'liq ⇒ after c. 1400 and Persianate. By place: Spain 720-1500; India after c. 1200; Southeast Asia after c. 1300; West Africa after c. 1100.
techniques.lookFor: Bands of script as the main ornament, with arabesque scrolls and star-polygon geometry; religious objects avoid figures. Kufic is blocky with a strong baseline; thuluth has tall verticals and sweeping curves; nasta'liq floats diagonally.
techniques.blurb: Abd al-Malik's Dome of the Rock (691-2) and reformed coinage (696) made writing the emblem of the new faith. The script style is as datable as Latin letterforms, and the map of its spread is the map of Islam.

techniques.name: La Tene 'Celtic' curvilinear style & Insular interlace

arrivals.note: continues to c. 100 CE; mirrors, shields, torcs

arrivals.place: Ireland & Northumbria (Insular revival: interlace, spirals, carpet pages)
arrivals.note: c. 650-900: Book of Kells, Tara brooch, high crosses

end.note: ends on the Continent with Roman conquest (c. 50 BCE) and in Britain by c. 100 CE; the Insular revival runs c. 650-900

techniques.rule: Swirling asymmetric tendrils, trumpets and triskeles on bronze or gold ⇒ Iron Age Europe c. 450 BCE-100 CE. Tight ribbon interlace with animal heads plus spirals ⇒ Insular, c. 650-900 CE (eras 500-750, 750-1000). Heavy twisted gold neck-rings (torcs) ⇒ c. 400-50 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: Flowing S-curves and comma leaves that hide faces, red enamel or coral studs, engraved basketry hatching. Insular work adds knotwork, key patterns, and biting beasts, on manuscripts, penannular brooches and stone crosses.
techniques.blurb: La Tene style grew from Greek and Etruscan plant ornament reinterpreted north of the Alps. Rome ended it on the Continent, but it survived in Ireland and re-emerged in Christian guise.

techniques.name: Viking animal styles (Oseberg to Urnes)

arrivals.place: British Isles (Danelaw, Isle of Man, Dublin)

end.note: Urnes style gives way to Romanesque

techniques.rule: Gripping beasts and ribbon animals on metalwork, wood or runestones ⇒ c. 790-1150 (eras 750-1000, 1000-1250). Sequence: Oseberg/Broa (c. 790-850), Borre (850-950), Jelling (900-975), Mammen (950-1025), Ringerike (1000-1075), Urnes (1050-1150). Runestones with serpent bands ⇒ mostly Sweden c. 980-1100.
techniques.lookFor: Contorted animals whose paws grip the frame (Borre), S-shaped ribbon beasts (Jelling), tendril-sprouting great beasts (Ringerike), ultra-slender looping greyhounds and snakes (Urnes); oval 'tortoise' brooches, Thor's hammers, silver arm-rings.
techniques.blurb: Viking art is one continuous animal ornament that changes fashion every half-century. Because the styles are dated by coin hoards and tree-ring-dated ships and buildings, they are unusually precise.

techniques.name: Steppe animal style (Scythian, Saka, Xiongnu)

arrivals.note: Greek-made gold for Scythian patrons from c. 400 BCE
belt plaques; influences Warring States and Han design
turquoise-inlaid, c. 200 BCE-100 CE

end.note: Scythian power ends c. 300-200 BCE; Sarmatian and Xiongnu variants continue to c. 200 CE

techniques.rule: Gold or bronze plaque of a coiled feline, stag with folded legs and flowing antlers, or predator-attacks-prey with twisted hindquarters ⇒ Eurasian steppe c. 800-200 BCE (eras 1000-750 BCE through 250-0 BCE). Naturalistic Greek-style scenes of Scythians on gold ⇒ c. 400-300 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: Compact, stylised animals with bodies bent to fill the shape, hindquarters rotated 180 degrees, beaks and antler tips turning into bird heads; small portable items: belt plaques, horse gear, dagger hilts.
techniques.blurb: The earliest kurgan at Arzhan in Tuva shows the style arose in the eastern steppe and moved west. It links objects from the Black Sea to the Great Wall across five centuries.

techniques.name: Renaissance all'antica style
techniques.rule: Classical columns, round arches, putti, grotesques, candelabra ornament, medallion portraits, nude mythological figures ⇒ Italy after c. 1420, the rest of Europe after c. 1490-1520. North of the Alps, anything before 1500 should still look Gothic (pointed arches, tracery, angular drapery).
techniques.lookFor: Symmetry, pilasters, shell niches, laurel wreaths, Roman capital lettering; 'grotesque' ornament of slender scrolls, masks and hybrid creatures appears after the Domus Aurea discoveries of c. 1480.
techniques.blurb: The classical revival was Italian for most of a century before the French invasions of 1494 and the print trade spread it. In northern and Iberian objects, Gothic and Renaissance ornament overlap c. 1500-1540.

techniques.name: Neoclassicism (and Empire / Egyptian revival)

end.note: merges into historicist revivals

techniques.rule: Straight tapered legs, urns, swags, Greek key, oval medallions, white cameo-like reliefs, togas ⇒ after c. 1760 (final era). Sphinxes, eagles, bees, gilt-bronze mounts on dark mahogany ⇒ Empire/Regency, 1800-1830. Curvy asymmetrical shell-work (Rococo) ⇒ c. 1730-1775.
techniques.lookFor: Rectilinear, symmetrical, pale colours, low relief in white on blue/green (Wedgwood), archaeological quotations from Pompeii; women in high-waisted white gowns c. 1795-1820.
techniques.blurb: The excavations of Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748) and Winckelmann's writings turned taste against Rococo within a decade. It is the default 'look' of the last decades of the 18th century on both sides of the Atlantic.

techniques.name: Chinoiserie

arrivals.note: via the Manila galleon

end.note: fades with Neoclassicism; brief Regency revival c. 1815-1830

techniques.rule: European-made object with fanciful 'Chinese' figures, pagodas, parasols and latticework ⇒ c. 1660-1790, peak 1740-1770 (eras 1500-1750 tail, 1750-2000 start). Conversely, Chinese-made objects in European shapes or with coats of arms ⇒ export ware, c. 1700-1850.
techniques.lookFor: Whimsical, inaccurate Asian scenes drawn by Europeans: mandarins with drooping moustaches, bells on pagoda roofs, exotic birds, on tin-glaze, porcelain, lacquered furniture, wallpaper and silver.
techniques.blurb: Chinoiserie is Europe's fantasy of Cathay, fed by East India Company imports. It rides on the back of the tea, porcelain and lacquer trades and dovetails with Rococo asymmetry.

techniques.name: Japonisme

end.note: absorbed into Art Nouveau and modernism

techniques.rule: Western object with asymmetrical compositions, cranes, bamboo, fans, cherry blossom, mon-like roundels, or flat ukiyo-e-style cropping ⇒ after Japan's opening (1854), in practice 1862-1915. Japanese objects made for this market (Satsuma ware, cloisonne, ivory okimono, bronzes) ⇒ Meiji, 1868-1912.
techniques.lookFor: Off-centre motifs wandering over the edge, large empty areas, mixed-metal inlays on silver, ebonised furniture with fretwork, dense gilded crackle-glazed Satsuma with tiny figures.
techniques.blurb: The 1862 London and 1867 Paris exhibitions set off a craze for Japan that reshaped Western design and painting. It also created a huge Japanese export-art industry aimed at Western buyers.

techniques.name: Europeans & European ships depicted in non-European art

arrivals.note: c. 1590-1640; Dutch at Dejima in later Nagasaki prints

techniques.rule: Figures with brimmed hats, long noses, beards, breeches, muskets, or three-masted ships with square sails in African, Asian, American or Pacific art ⇒ after first contact: c. 1485 West Africa, 1498 India, 1519 Mexico, 1543 Japan, 1770s Pacific. All such pieces are era 1250-1500 (tail) or later.
techniques.lookFor: Benin plaques: Portuguese with helmets, matchlocks and manillas. Nanban screens: tall carracks, baggy bombacha trousers, black attendants, Jesuits. Mughal pages: copies of European Madonnas and angels.
techniques.blurb: The Age of Exploration is visible from the other side: local artists recorded the newcomers within a few years of their arrival, giving a precise lower bound for each region.

techniques.name: Domestic horse

arrivals.note: cavalry states of Mali and Songhai; tsetse fly limits horses in the forest zone
spread after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680

techniques.rule: Horse depicted or horse gear present ⇒ after c. 2000 BCE in West Asia, c. 1650 BCE in Egypt (not Old or Middle Kingdom), c. 1250 BCE in China, 1493+ in the Americas, c. 1700+ for Plains tribes. Horse riding (as opposed to chariots) in art becomes common only after c. 900 BCE.
techniques.lookFor: Distinguish horses from the onagers and donkeys of earlier Mesopotamian art (long ears, tufted tail). Plains ledger drawings and beaded horse gear are 19th century. West African equestrian figures ⇒ Sahel after c. 1000 CE.
techniques.blurb: Genetics now places the origin of the modern domestic horse on the lower Volga-Don steppe around 2200 BCE, spreading explosively with chariots. The Americas had no horses from the Ice Age until Columbus's second voyage.

techniques.name: Domestic camels

arrivals.note: two-humped camel, separately domesticated
rare before the Persian period; common from Ptolemaic times
tomb figures from Han, plentiful in Northern Wei and Tang
makes regular trans-Saharan trade possible

techniques.rule: Dromedary depicted ⇒ after c. 1000 BCE and essentially never in pharaonic Egyptian art; in North Africa and the Sahara ⇒ after c. 300 CE. Two-humped camel figure ⇒ Central Asia or China, and in China overwhelmingly c. 400-800 CE (Northern Wei to Tang).
techniques.lookFor: Count the humps: one = Arabian (Near East, Africa, India); two = Bactrian (Iran to China). Tang camels bray with raised heads and carry saddle-packs with monster masks.
techniques.blurb: The dromedary is a late domesticate (estimates run from c. 2000 to c. 1000 BCE, with pack use common only from about 1000 BCE), and it reached Egypt and the Sahara later still. Its arrival remade desert trade and, for the game, is a reliable 'no earlier than' marker.

techniques.name: New World crops in the Old World (maize, chili, tomato, potato, cacao)

arrivals.place: Italy (maize painted in the Villa Farnesina festoons)

techniques.rule: Maize cobs, chili peppers, tomatoes, potatoes, pumpkins/squash, pineapples, sunflowers, turkeys or cacao pods in Old World art ⇒ after 1493 (era 1250-1500's last years or later; realistically 1500+). Conversely wheat, grapes, cattle, sheep, pigs, chickens, sugar cane or citrus in American art ⇒ after 1492.
techniques.lookFor: Look in still-lifes, botanical borders, garlands, carved capitals and ceramic shapes: maize ears with husks, gourd-shaped vessels, turkey figures. Chocolate pots have a hole in the lid for a stirring rod.
techniques.blurb: The Columbian Exchange is a hard horizon for plants and animals in art. Maize is painted in Rome by 1517; chili reaches India and China within the century.

techniques.name: Tobacco pipes, hookahs & snuff bottles outside the Americas

arrivals.note: tobacco known from Portuguese contact; pipe smoking widespread by c. 1600
archaeologists use pipes to date sites to after c. 1600
Qing court fashion; most bottles 1750-1920

techniques.rule: Smoking pipe, hookah/water-pipe base, tobacco jar, snuffbox or snuff bottle from Europe, Asia or Africa ⇒ after c. 1575-1600 (era 1500-1750 or later). Chinese snuff bottle ⇒ after c. 1700. Bidri or glass huqqa bases ⇒ India after c. 1620. Native American stone pipes may be far older (Hopewell platform pipes c. 100 BCE-400 CE).
techniques.lookFor: European clay pipes: tiny bowls early (c. 1600), larger and more upright by 1700+. Hookah bases: globular then bell-shaped (after c. 1730). Snuff bottles: small flask with a stopper-spoon, in glass, jade, agate, porcelain, inside-painted glass (after c. 1880).
techniques.blurb: Tobacco went round the world in about a century and generated a whole new class of datable objects. A person smoking in an Old World picture places it after the late 16th century.

techniques.name: Glass trade beads & seed-bead embroidery

arrivals.place: South India & Sri Lanka (Indo-Pacific drawn beads)
arrivals.note: earlier, separate industry supplying Africa and Southeast Asia to c. 1500
Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe, Swahili coast
tiny 'seed' beads and full beaded surfaces after c. 1840

techniques.rule: Solid beadwork in small uniform glass beads on Native American, African, Arctic or Bornean objects ⇒ after European trade and in practice 1800-1950 (final era). Plains: quillwork and few large 'pony' beads before c. 1840; dense seed-bead designs after; floral designs after c. 1870. No glass in the pre-Columbian Americas.
techniques.lookFor: Tiny regular glass beads sewn in lanes (lazy stitch) or flat appliqué in white, sky blue, dark blue, red (white-heart) and greasy yellow; on hide, cloth or fibre. Venetian chevron and millefiori beads are larger and striped.
techniques.blurb: Venetian, Dutch and Bohemian factories exported beads by the ton as currency for the fur, ivory and slave trades. Whole art forms, from Lakota moccasins to Zulu love letters, are therefore 19th-century creations.

techniques.name: Dong Son bronze drums

arrivals.place: Yunnan (Dian kingdom cowrie containers and drums)

arrivals.note: drum casting continues among southern minorities into the Qing
Pejeng-type drums cast locally
Heger III type, made until the early 20th c.

end.note: classic Heger I drums end in the early centuries CE after Han conquest; later types continue

techniques.rule: Kettle-shaped bronze drum with a central star, rings of flying birds, feathered warriors and boats ⇒ Dong Son, c. 600 BCE-200 CE (eras 750-500 BCE through 0-250 CE), found from Vietnam to eastern Indonesia. Thin drums with rows of small frogs on the rim and plain bands ⇒ Karen type, 1000-1900 CE.
techniques.lookFor: Flat tympanum with a 10-16 point star, concentric geometric bands, a bulging shoulder, straight waist and flared foot, four strap handles, cast in one piece by lost wax.
techniques.blurb: Dong Son drums are the signature of Southeast Asia's Bronze-Iron Age and were traded by sea across the archipelago. Their imagery of longboats and plumed dancers is the best picture of that world.

techniques.name: Eyeglasses

arrivals.note: imports via Malacca and Central Asia

techniques.rule: Spectacles on a figure or as an object ⇒ after 1286; in art after c. 1350 (era 1250-1500 or later). Rivet or arch-bridge glasses perched on the nose with no arms ⇒ c. 1300-1730; rigid side arms ⇒ after c. 1727; pince-nez ⇒ c. 1840-1920.
techniques.lookFor: Two round lenses joined by a rivet or arched bridge, held by hand or pinched on the nose; scholars, saints (Jerome, apostles) and notaries wear them in 15th-century paintings.
techniques.blurb: Reading glasses were invented in Italy in the 1280s; a friar preaching in 1306 said the art was less than twenty years old. Side arms took four more centuries.

techniques.name: Lapita pottery & the settlement of Remote Oceania

arrivals.note: date debated; c. 900-1150 on current radiocarbon
estimates range c. 1000-1250
moai carved mostly c. 1250-1500

techniques.rule: Dentate-stamped Lapita pottery ⇒ c. 1500-500 BCE, western Pacific. Any artefact from East Polynesia ⇒ after c. 1000 CE; Hawai'i after c. 1000-1200; Rapa Nui after c. 1200; New Zealand (Maori) after c. 1280. Polynesia east of Samoa has no pottery at all, and most museum pieces date from 1770-1900.
techniques.lookFor: Lapita: red-slipped sherds with fine comb-tooth stamped bands, faces and interlocking geometric motifs, sometimes lime-filled. East Polynesian objects are wood, stone, bone, shell, fibre and feathers; no metal before contact.
techniques.blurb: The Lapita people crossed from the Bismarcks to Samoa in a few centuries, then paused for nearly two thousand years before their descendants swept through East Polynesia. New Zealand was the last large landmass settled by humans.
